title: 5-HT3 antagonists – Mechanism of action and primary use
content: 5-HT3 antagonists are antiemetics used mainly in the management of chemotherapy-related nausea. They act primarily in the chemoreceptor trigger zone area of the medulla oblongata.

title: 5-HT3 antagonists – Examples and drug-specific notes
content: Examples include ondansetron and palonosetron. Palonosetron is a second-generation 5-HT3 antagonist whose main advantage is a reduced effect on the QT interval compared to first-generation agents.

title: 5-HT3 antagonists – Adverse effects
content: Adverse effects include prolonged QT interval and constipation (common).

title: Aphasia – Wernicke's (receptive) aphasia
content: Due to a lesion of the superior temporal gyrus, typically supplied by the inferior division of the left MCA. This area forms speech before sending it to Broca's area. Lesions result in sentences that make no sense, word substitution and neologisms but speech remains fluent ('word salad'). Comprehension is impaired.

title: Aphasia – Broca's (expressive) aphasia
content: Due to a lesion of the inferior frontal gyrus, typically supplied by the superior division of the left MCA. Speech is non-fluent, laboured, and halting. Repetition is impaired. Comprehension is normal.

title: Aphasia – Conduction aphasia
content: Classically due to a stroke affecting the arcuate fasciculus — the connection between Wernicke's and Broca's area. Speech is fluent but repetition is poor. The patient is aware of the errors they are making. Comprehension is normal.

title: Aphasia – Global aphasia
content: A large lesion affecting all three areas (Wernicke's, Broca's, and arcuate fasciculus) results in severe expressive and receptive aphasia. The patient may still be able to communicate using gestures.

title: Arnold-Chiari malformation – Definition and features
content: Arnold-Chiari malformation describes the downward displacement (herniation) of the cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum. Malformations may be congenital or acquired through trauma. Features include non-communicating hydrocephalus (from obstruction of CSF outflow), headache, and syringomyelia.

title: Ataxia – Cerebellar localisation
content: Cerebellar hemisphere lesions cause peripheral ataxia ('finger-nose ataxia'). Cerebellar vermis lesions cause gait ataxia.

title: Ataxia telangiectasia – Definition and genetics
content: Ataxia telangiectasia is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a defect in the ATM gene which encodes for DNA repair enzymes. It is one of the inherited combined immunodeficiency disorders, typically presenting in early childhood with abnormal movements.

title: Ataxia telangiectasia – Clinical features
content: Features include cerebellar ataxia, telangiectasia (spider angiomas), IgA deficiency resulting in recurrent chest infections, and a 10% risk of developing malignancy (lymphoma or leukaemia, but also non-lymphoid tumours).

title: Autonomic dysreflexia – Pathophysiology and triggers
content: Occurs in patients with spinal cord injury at or above T6. Afferent signals (most commonly from faecal impaction or urinary retention) trigger a sympathetic spinal reflex via thoracolumbar outflow. The usual centrally mediated parasympathetic response is prevented by the cord lesion, resulting in an unbalanced physiological response.

title: Autonomic dysreflexia – Clinical features
content: Characterised by extreme hypertension, flushing and sweating above the level of the cord lesion, and agitation. In untreated cases, severe consequences of extreme hypertension have been reported, including haemorrhagic stroke.

title: Autonomic dysreflexia – Management
content: Management involves removal or control of the triggering stimulus and treatment of any life-threatening hypertension and/or bradycardia.

title: Autonomic neuropathy – Definition and pathophysiology
content: Autonomic neuropathy describes dysfunction of the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems, leading to impaired cardiovascular, genitourinary, gastrointestinal and sudomotor regulation. Damage affects small myelinated and unmyelinated autonomic fibres via metabolic, immune-mediated, neurodegenerative, infective or drug-induced mechanisms.

title: Autonomic neuropathy – Clinical features
content: Features include postural hypotension (≥30/15 mmHg drop), reduced or absent heart rate variability with deep breathing (an earlier and more sensitive sign than BP changes), erectile dysfunction, impaired sweating or anhidrosis, gastroparesis (early satiety, nausea, bloating), and pupillary denervation hypersensitivity (dilates with adrenaline).

title: Autonomic neuropathy – Causes
content: Causes include diabetes (most common), Guillain-Barré syndrome, multiple system atrophy/Shy-Drager syndrome, Parkinson's disease, infections (HIV, Chagas' disease, neurosyphilis), drugs (antihypertensives, tricyclic antidepressants), and structural lesions (craniopharyngioma).

title: Autonomic neuropathy – Investigations
content: Investigations include cardiovascular autonomic tests (HR variability, lying/standing BP), sweat testing (QSART or thermoregulatory), pupillary pharmacological testing, blood tests (HbA1c, B12, autoimmune screen, HIV, syphilis), MRI brain/spine if central pathology suspected, and nerve conduction studies with small-fibre assessments. In autonomic neuropathy, the classical finding is denervation hypersensitivity of the iris dilator muscle.

title: Autonomic neuropathy – Management
content: Treat underlying cause (optimise glycaemic control, stop offending drugs, treat infections). For postural hypotension: conservative measures (fluids, salt, compression stockings, slow positional changes) then fludrocortisone or midodrine. Erectile dysfunction: PDE5 inhibitors. Sweat dysfunction: moisturisers, temperature regulation. MDT input including neurology, physiotherapy and occupational therapy.

title: Bell's palsy – Definition and epidemiology
content: Bell's palsy is an acute, unilateral, idiopathic facial nerve paralysis. The aetiology is unknown although the role of herpes simplex virus has been investigated. Peak incidence is 20–40 years and the condition is more common in pregnant women.

title: Bell's palsy – Clinical features
content: Presents with lower motor neuron facial nerve palsy (forehead affected). In contrast, an upper motor neuron lesion spares the upper face. Additional features include post-auricular pain (may precede paralysis), altered taste, dry eyes, and hyperacusis.

title: Bell's palsy – Management
content: All patients should receive oral prednisolone within 72 hours of onset. There is ongoing debate about adding antiviral medications; antiviral treatment alone is not recommended. UpToDate recommends addition of antivirals for severe facial palsy. Eye care is important to prevent exposure keratopathy: prescribe artificial tears and eye lubricants; if unable to close the eye at bedtime, tape it closed using microporous tape.

title: Bell's palsy – Follow-up and prognosis
content: If paralysis shows no sign of improvement after 3 weeks, refer urgently to ENT. A referral to plastic surgery may be appropriate for more long-standing weakness (e.g. several months). Most patients make a full recovery within 3–4 months. If untreated, around 15% of patients have permanent moderate to severe weakness.

title: Brachial plexus – Anatomy and origin
content: The brachial plexus arises from anterior rami of C5 to T1. Sections of the plexus (mnemonic: Real Teenagers Drink Cold Beer): Roots (posterior triangle, between scalenus anterior and medius), Trunks (posterior to middle third of clavicle), Divisions (apex of axilla), Cords (related to axillary artery), Branches.

title: Brachial plexus injuries – Erb-Duchenne paralysis
content: Erb-Duchenne paralysis results from damage to C5 and C6 roots. Features include winged scapula and may be caused by a breech presentation.

title: Brachial plexus injuries – Klumpke's paralysis
content: Klumpke's paralysis results from damage to T1. Features include loss of intrinsic hand muscles and is due to traction.

title: Brain abscess – Causes and pathogenesis
content: Brain abscesses may result from extension of sepsis from middle ear or sinuses, trauma or surgery to the scalp, penetrating head injuries, or embolic events from endocarditis.

title: Brain abscess – Clinical features
content: Presenting symptoms depend on the site of the abscess. Features include headache (often dull and persistent), fever (may be absent; usually not the swinging pyrexia seen at other sites), focal neurology (e.g. oculomotor or abducens nerve palsy from raised ICP), nausea, papilloedema, and seizures.

title: Brain abscess – Management
content: Management includes surgery (craniotomy with debridement of the abscess cavity), IV antibiotics (IV 3rd-generation cephalosporin + metronidazole), and intracranial pressure management with dexamethasone.

title: Brain lesions – Parietal lobe features
content: Parietal lobe lesions cause sensory inattention, apraxias, astereognosis (tactile agnosia), inferior homonymous quadrantanopia, and Gerstmann's syndrome (dominant parietal): alexia, acalculia, finger agnosia and right-left disorientation.

title: Brain lesions – Occipital lobe features
content: Occipital lobe lesions cause homonymous hemianopia (with macula sparing), cortical blindness, and visual agnosia.

title: Brain lesions – Temporal lobe features
content: Temporal lobe lesions cause Wernicke's aphasia (fluent speech with word substitution and neologisms), superior homonymous quadrantanopia, auditory agnosia, and prosopagnosia (difficulty recognising faces).

title: Brain lesions – Frontal lobe features
content: Frontal lobe lesions cause expressive (Broca's) aphasia (non-fluent, laboured, halting speech), disinhibition, perseveration, anosmia, and inability to generate a list.

title: Brain lesions – Cerebellar features
content: Midline cerebellar lesions cause gait and truncal ataxia. Hemisphere lesions cause intention tremor, past pointing, dysdiadochokinesis, and nystagmus.

title: Brain lesions – Specific subcortical area localisation
content: Medial thalamus and mammillary bodies → Wernicke and Korsakoff syndrome. Subthalamic nucleus of basal ganglia → hemiballism. Striatum (caudate nucleus) → Huntington's chorea. Substantia nigra → Parkinson's disease. Amygdala → Kluver-Bucy syndrome (hypersexuality, hyperorality, hyperphagia, visual agnosia).

title: Brain tumours – Overview and classification
content: The majority of adult tumours are supratentorial, whereas the majority of childhood tumours are infratentorial. Metastatic brain cancer is the most common form of brain tumour overall; they are often multiple and not treatable with surgical intervention. Tumours most commonly spreading to the brain: lung (most common), breast, bowel, skin (melanoma), kidney.

title: Brain tumours – Glioblastoma multiforme
content: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) is the most common primary tumour in adults with a poor prognosis (~1 year). On imaging: solid tumours with central necrosis and a contrast-enhancing rim, associated with vasogenic oedema. Histology: pleomorphic tumour cells bordering necrotic areas. Treatment: surgical resection with postoperative chemotherapy and/or radiotherapy; dexamethasone for oedema.

title: Brain tumours – Meningioma
content: The second most common primary brain tumour in adults. Typically benign, extrinsic tumours arising from arachnoid cap cells, located next to the dura. Common locations: falx cerebri, superior sagittal sinus, convexity or skull base. Histology: spindle cells in concentric whorls and calcified psammoma bodies. Investigation: CT (contrast enhancement) and MRI. Treatment: observation, radiotherapy or surgical resection.

title: Brain tumours – Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma)
content: A benign tumour arising from the eighth cranial nerve (vestibulocochlear nerve), often in the cerebellopontine angle. Presents with hearing loss, facial nerve palsy (compression of nearby facial nerve), and tinnitus. Associated with neurofibromatosis type 2 (bilateral vestibular schwannomas). Histology: Antoni A or B patterns; Verocay bodies (acellular areas surrounded by nuclear palisades). Treatment: observation, radiotherapy or surgery.

title: Brain tumours – Pilocytic astrocytoma
content: The most common primary brain tumour in children. Histology: Rosenthal fibres (corkscrew eosinophilic bundles).

title: Brain tumours – Medulloblastoma
content: An aggressive paediatric brain tumour arising within the infratentorial compartment. Spreads through the CSF system. Treatment: surgical resection and chemotherapy. Histology: small blue cells in a rosette pattern with many mitotic figures.

title: Brain tumours – Other primary brain tumours
content: Ependymoma: commonly in the 4th ventricle, may cause hydrocephalus; histology: perivascular pseudorosettes. Oligodendroglioma: benign, slow-growing, common in frontal lobes; histology: calcifications with 'fried-egg' appearance. Haemangioblastoma: vascular tumour of the cerebellum, associated with von Hippel-Lindau syndrome; histology: foam cells and high vascularity.

title: Brain tumours – Pituitary adenoma
content: Benign tumours of the pituitary gland, either secretory (producing a hormone in excess) or non-secretory. Divided into microadenomas (<1 cm) and macroadenomas (>1 cm). Patients present with consequences of hormone excess (e.g. Cushing's from ACTH, acromegaly from GH) or depletion. Compression of the optic chiasm causes bitemporal hemianopia. Investigation: pituitary blood profile and MRI. Treatment: hormonal or surgical (transphenoidal resection).

title: Brain tumours – Craniopharyngioma
content: Most common paediatric supratentorial tumour. A solid/cystic tumour of the sellar region derived from remnants of Rathke's pouch. Common in children but can present in adults. May present with hormonal disturbance, symptoms of hydrocephalus, or bitemporal hemianopia. Investigation: pituitary blood profile and MRI. Treatment: surgical with or without postoperative radiotherapy.

title: Brown-Séquard syndrome – Pathophysiology and features
content: Caused by lateral hemisection of the spinal cord. Features: ipsilateral weakness below the lesion (lateral corticospinal tract), ipsilateral loss of proprioception and vibration sensation (dorsal columns), and contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation (lateral spinothalamic tract).

title: Carbamazepine – Mechanism of action and uses
content: Carbamazepine binds to sodium channels, increasing their refractory period. It is used for focal seizures (second-line), trigeminal neuralgia (first-line), and bipolar disorder. It exhibits autoinduction — patients may experience a return of seizures after 3–4 weeks of treatment.

title: Carbamazepine – Adverse effects
content: Adverse effects include: P450 enzyme induction, dizziness and ataxia, drowsiness, headache, visual disturbances (especially diplopia), Stevens-Johnson syndrome, leucopenia and agranulocytosis, and hyponatraemia secondary to SIADH.

title: Cataplexy – Definition and association
content: Cataplexy describes the sudden and transient loss of muscular tone caused by strong emotion (e.g. laughter, being frightened). Features range from buckling knees to complete collapse. Around two-thirds of patients with narcolepsy have cataplexy.

title: Cavernous sinus – Anatomy and contents
content: The cavernous sinuses are paired, situated on the body of the sphenoid bone, running from the superior orbital fissure to the petrous temporal bone. Lateral wall (top to bottom): oculomotor nerve (III), trochlear nerve (IV), ophthalmic nerve (V1), maxillary nerve (V2). Within the sinus (medial to lateral): internal carotid artery with sympathetic plexus, abducens nerve (VI). Drains into the internal jugular vein via superior and inferior petrosal sinuses.

title: Cerebellar syndrome – Clinical features (DANISH+V)
content: Mnemonic DANISH+V: Dysdiadochokinesia and Dysmetria (past-pointing), Ataxia (limb and truncal), Nystagmus (horizontal = ipsilateral hemisphere), Intention tremor, Slurred staccato speech (scanning dysarthria), Hypotonia, Vertigo/vestibular features (imbalance, dizziness, nausea, vomiting — most likely when flocculonodular lobe affected). Unilateral cerebellar lesions cause ipsilateral signs.

title: Cerebellar syndrome – Causes
content: Causes include: Friedreich's ataxia, ataxia telangiectasia, neoplastic (cerebellar haemangioma), stroke, alcohol, multiple sclerosis, hypothyroidism, drugs (phenytoin, lead poisoning), and paraneoplastic (e.g. secondary to lung cancer).

title: Cerebral perfusion pressure – Definition and formula
content: Cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) is the net pressure gradient causing blood flow to the brain. CPP = Mean arterial pressure − Intracranial pressure. A sharp rise in CPP may result in a rising ICP; a fall in CPP may result in cerebral ischaemia. Following trauma, CPP must be carefully controlled with invasive monitoring.

title: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis – Overview and risk factors
content: Can cause cerebral infarction; 50% of patients have isolated sagittal sinus thromboses. Risk factors include prothrombotic states (inherited/acquired thrombophilias), hormonal factors (pregnancy, postpartum, oestrogen-containing drugs), local infections (otitis media → lateral sinus; sinusitis → cavernous sinus; meningitis), severe dehydration, and head trauma or neurosurgery.

title: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis – Investigations and management
content: MRI venography is the gold standard; CT venography is an alternative. Non-contrast CT head is normal in around 70% of patients. D-dimer levels may be elevated. Management: anticoagulation — typically low molecular weight heparin acutely, then warfarin for longer-term anticoagulation.

title: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis – Sagittal sinus thrombosis
content: Sagittal sinus thrombosis may present with seizures and hemiplegia. Parasagittal biparietal or bifrontal haemorrhagic infarctions may be seen. The 'empty delta sign' is seen on venography.

title: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis – Cavernous sinus thrombosis
content: Features include periorbital erythema and oedema, ophthalmoplegia (6th nerve damage typically occurs before 3rd and 4th), trigeminal nerve involvement (hyperaesthesia of upper face and eye pain), and central retinal vein thrombosis. Other causes of cavernous sinus syndrome: local infection (e.g. sinusitis), neoplasia, trauma.

title: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis – Lateral sinus thrombosis
content: Lateral sinus thrombosis presents with 6th and 7th cranial nerve palsies.

title: Common peroneal nerve palsy – Causes and features
content: The most common cause of foot drop. Often secondary to compression at the neck of the fibula from leg crossing, squatting, kneeling, prolonged confinement, recent weight loss, Baker's cysts, or plaster casts. Features: weakness of foot dorsiflexion and eversion, weakness of extensor hallucis longus, sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot and lower lateral leg, wasting of anterior tibial and peroneal muscles. Reflexes are normal.

title: Common peroneal nerve palsy vs L5 radiculopathy – Distinguishing features
content: Common peroneal nerve palsy vs L5 radiculopathy: Foot inversion — preserved vs weak. Hip abduction (gluteus medius) — normal vs weak. Back/radicular pain — absent vs present. Sensory pattern — dorsum of foot ± lateral shin vs L5 dermatome (lateral leg → dorsum foot → big toe).

title: Cranial nerves – Overview and mnemonic
content: There are 12 cranial nerves. Mnemonic for modality (S=Sensory, M=Motor, B=Both): 'Some Say Marry Money But My Brother Says Big Brains Matter Most' (CN I–XII). CN I: Olfactory (smell, cribriform plate). CN II: Optic (sight, optic canal). CN XI: Accessory (head/shoulder movement, jugular foramen). CN XII: Hypoglossal (tongue movement — deviates towards side of lesion, hypoglossal canal).

title: Cranial nerves – CN III (Oculomotor) palsy
content: CN III supplies eye movement (MR, IO, SR, IR), pupil constriction, accommodation, and eyelid opening. Palsy results in ptosis, 'down and out' eye position, and a dilated, fixed pupil. Passes through the superior orbital fissure.

title: Cranial nerves – CN IV (Trochlear) palsy
content: CN IV supplies the superior oblique muscle (eye movement). Palsy results in defective downward gaze and vertical diplopia, classically noticed when reading or going downstairs. Passes through the superior orbital fissure.

title: Cranial nerves – CN V (Trigeminal) lesions
content: CN V provides facial sensation and innervates mastication. Lesions may cause trigeminal neuralgia, loss of corneal reflex (afferent limb), loss of facial sensation, paralysis of mastication muscles, and deviation of jaw to the weak side. V1 passes through SOF, V2 through foramen rotundum, V3 through foramen ovale.

title: Cranial nerves – CN VI (Abducens) palsy
content: CN VI supplies the lateral rectus (eye movement). Palsy results in defective abduction and horizontal diplopia. Passes through the superior orbital fissure.

title: Cranial nerves – CN VII (Facial) lesions
content: CN VII provides facial movement, taste (anterior 2/3 of tongue), lacrimation, and salivation. Lesions result in flaccid paralysis of upper and lower face, loss of corneal reflex (efferent limb), loss of taste, and hyperacusis. Passes through the internal auditory meatus.

title: Cranial nerves – CN VIII (Vestibulocochlear) lesions
content: CN VIII provides hearing and balance. Lesions cause hearing loss, vertigo, and nystagmus. Acoustic neuromas are Schwann cell tumours of the cochlear nerve. Passes through the internal auditory meatus.

title: Cranial nerves – CN IX, X, XI lesions
content: CN IX (Glossopharyngeal): taste (posterior 1/3 tongue), salivation, swallowing; lesions cause hypersensitive carotid sinus reflex and loss of gag reflex (afferent). CN X (Vagus): phonation, swallowing, visceral innervation; lesions cause uvula deviation away from lesion and loss of gag reflex (efferent). CN XI (Accessory): head and shoulder movement; lesions cause weakness turning head to contralateral side. All pass through the jugular foramen.

title: Cranial nerve reflexes – Summary
content: Corneal reflex: afferent V1, efferent VII. Jaw jerk: afferent and efferent V3. Gag reflex: afferent IX, efferent X. Carotid sinus reflex: afferent IX, efferent X. Pupillary light reflex: afferent II, efferent III. Lacrimation reflex: afferent V1, efferent VII.

title: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease – Pathophysiology and types
content: CJD is a rapidly progressive neurological condition caused by prion proteins that induce amyloid folds forming tightly packed beta-pleated sheets resistant to proteases. Sporadic CJD: 85% of cases, mean onset 65 years, 10–15% familial. New variant CJD: younger patients (average onset 25 years), psychological symptoms (anxiety, withdrawal, dysphonia) are most common presenting features, methionine homozygosity at codon 129 is a risk factor, median survival 13 months.

title: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease – Investigations
content: CSF is usually normal. EEG: biphasic, high amplitude sharp waves (only in sporadic CJD). MRI: hyperintense signals in the basal ganglia and thalamus. Clinical features include rapid-onset dementia and myoclonus.

title: Degenerative cervical myelopathy – Risk factors and presentation
content: Risk factors include smoking (effects on intervertebral discs), genetics, and occupation (high axial loading). Presentation is variable and often subtle early on. Symptoms include pain (neck, upper or lower limbs), loss of motor function (loss of digital dexterity, arm/leg weakness/stiffness, impaired gait), loss of sensory function (numbness), and loss of autonomic function (urinary or faecal incontinence, impotence). Hoffman's sign is positive in cervical myelopathy.

title: Degenerative cervical myelopathy – Investigations and management
content: MRI of the cervical spine is the gold standard investigation. It may reveal disc degeneration, ligament hypertrophy, and cord signal change. All patients should be urgently referred for specialist spinal services (neurosurgery or orthopaedic spinal surgery). Decompressive surgery is the only effective treatment; it prevents disease progression. Early treatment (within 6 months of diagnosis) offers the best chance of full recovery. Physiotherapy should only be initiated by specialist services as manipulation can cause more cord damage.

title: Dermatomes – Key landmarks
content: Key dermatome landmarks: C2 (posterior skull cap), C3 (high turtleneck), C4 (low-collar shirt), C6 (thumb + index finger), C7 (middle finger + palm), C8 (ring + little finger), T4 (nipples), T10 (umbilicus), L1 (inguinal ligament), L4 (knee caps), L5 (big toe, dorsum of foot), S1 (lateral foot, small toe), S2–S3 (genitalia).

title: Drugs causing peripheral neuropathy
content: Drugs causing peripheral neuropathy include: amiodarone, isoniazid, vincristine, nitrofurantoin, and metronidazole.

title: DVLA neurological disorders – Epilepsy driving rules
content: All patients with epilepsy must not drive and must inform the DVLA. First unprovoked/isolated seizure: 6 months off (12 months if structural brain abnormality or definite epileptiform EEG activity). Established epilepsy: may drive if seizure-free for 12 months. A 'til 70 licence is usually restored after 5 seizure-free years on medication. Withdrawal of epilepsy medication: must not drive during withdrawal and for 6 months after the last dose.

title: DVLA neurological disorders – Syncope and other conditions
content: Syncope driving restrictions: simple faint (no restriction), single explained and treated episode (4 weeks off), single unexplained episode (6 months off), two or more episodes (12 months off). Stroke or TIA: 1 month off. Multiple TIAs over short period: 3 months off. Craniotomy for meningioma: 1 year off (6 months if benign and seizure-free). Narcolepsy/cataplexy: cease driving on diagnosis, restart when satisfactory symptom control. Chronic neurological disorders (MS, MND): inform DVLA, complete PK1 form.

title: Duchenne muscular dystrophy – Genetics and pathophysiology
content: X-linked recessive disorder due to a frameshift mutation in the dystrophin gene on Xp21. The frameshift results in loss of one or both binding sites of dystrophin (a membrane-associated protein connecting the muscle membrane to actin), leading to a severe phenotype. Becker muscular dystrophy is caused by a non-frameshift insertion, preserving both binding sites and resulting in a milder form.

title: Duchenne muscular dystrophy – Clinical features
content: Progressive proximal muscle weakness from age 5 years, calf pseudohypertrophy, Gower's sign (child uses arms to stand up from a squatted position), and 30% of patients have intellectual impairment.

title: Epilepsy – Classification of seizures
content: New classification based on 3 features: (1) where seizures begin, (2) level of awareness, (3) other features. Focal seizures (previously partial): start in one area, may be focal aware (previously simple partial), focal impaired awareness (previously complex partial), or awareness unknown; further classified as motor (e.g. Jacksonian march) or non-motor (e.g. déjà vu). Generalised: engage both sides at onset, consciousness lost immediately; subtypes include tonic-clonic, tonic, clonic, typical absence (petit mal), myoclonic, atonic. Focal to bilateral: previously secondary generalised seizures.

title: Epilepsy – Childhood epilepsy syndromes
content: West's syndrome (infantile spasms): brief flexion-extension spasms in first months of life, progressive mental handicap, EEG hypsarrhythmia, usually secondary to serious neurological abnormality, poor prognosis. Lennox-Gastaut syndrome: onset 1–5 years, atypical absences/falls/jerks, 90% moderate-severe mental handicap, EEG slow spike, ketogenic diet may help. Benign rolandic epilepsy: paraesthesia, seizures at night. Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (Janz syndrome): onset in teens, more common in girls, infrequent generalised seizures (often morning), daytime absences, myoclonic jerks; usually good response to sodium valproate.

title: Epilepsy – Febrile convulsions
content: Febrile convulsions typically occur in children aged 6 months to 5 years; around 3% of children will have at least one. They usually occur early in a viral infection as the temperature rises rapidly. Seizures are typically brief and generalised tonic or tonic-clonic in nature.

title: Epilepsy – Focal seizure localising features
content: Temporal lobe: aura (typically rising epigastric sensation, also déjà vu, jamais vu, auditory/gustatory/olfactory hallucinations), seizures last ~1 minute, automatisms (lip smacking, grabbing, plucking). Frontal lobe (motor): head/leg movements, posturing, post-ictal weakness, Jacksonian march. Parietal lobe (sensory): paraesthesia. Occipital lobe (visual): floaters/flashes.

title: Epilepsy – Treatment initiation and antiepileptic drugs
content: Most neurologists start antiepileptics after a second seizure. NICE recommends starting after the first seizure if: neurological deficit, structural brain abnormality on imaging, unequivocal epileptic EEG activity, or patient/family considers risk of further seizure unacceptable. Antiepileptics should be prescribed by brand due to bioavailability differences. Sodium valproate: increases GABA activity; no longer first-line; teratogenic (neural tube defects). Lamotrigine: sodium channel blocker; used for various generalised and focal seizures; adverse effect: Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

title: Epilepsy – Sodium valproate safety restrictions
content: Valproate must not be started for the first time in people (male or female) younger than 55 years, unless 2 specialists independently consider and document that there is no other effective or tolerated treatment, or there are compelling reasons that the reproductive risks do not apply. Adverse effects: teratogenicity (neural tube defects, neurodevelopmental delay), P450 inhibition, nausea, weight gain, alopecia, ataxia, tremor, hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, thrombocytopaenia, hyponatraemia, hyperammonaemic encephalopathy (treat with L-carnitine).

title: Epilepsy – Phenytoin mechanism and adverse effects
content: Phenytoin binds to sodium channels increasing their refractory period. No longer used first-line due to side-effect profile. Acute effects: dizziness, diplopia, nystagmus, slurred speech, ataxia; later confusion and seizures. Chronic effects: gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, coarsening of facial features, drowsiness, megaloblastic anaemia, peripheral neuropathy, osteomalacia (enhanced vitamin D metabolism), lymphadenopathy, dyskinesia. Idiosyncratic: fever, rashes (including toxic epidermal necrolysis), hepatitis, Dupuytren's contracture, aplastic anaemia, drug-induced lupus. Teratogenic: cleft palate and congenital heart disease. P450 enzyme inducer.

title: Epilepsy – Acute seizure management
content: Check airway, apply oxygen, place in recovery position. If prolonged, give benzodiazepines: rectal diazepam (adult 10–20 mg, max 30 mg) or buccal midazolam (adult 10 mg). Status epilepticus (single seizure >5 minutes or ≥2 seizures within 5 minutes without return to normal): medical emergency. In hospital: IV lorazepam (may repeat once after 5–10 minutes). If ongoing: second-line agent (levetiracetam, phenytoin, or sodium valproate — NICE notes levetiracetam may be quicker and have fewer adverse effects). Refractory status (failure of benzo + one second-line agent within 30–60 minutes): ITU, general anaesthesia (propofol, thiopentone, or midazolam infusion), continuous EEG monitoring.

title: Foot drop – Management
content: If isolated peroneal neuropathy is confirmed, conservative management is appropriate. Leg crossing, squatting, and kneeling should be avoided. Symptoms typically improve over 2–3 months. Bilateral symptoms, fasciculations, or other abnormal neurological findings (e.g. hyperreflexia) are indications for specialist referral.

title: Fourth nerve palsy – Clinical features
content: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) supplies the superior oblique muscle, enabling the eye to look down when adducted. Palsy features: vertical diplopia (classically noticed when reading or going downstairs), subjective tilting of objects (torsional diplopia), head tilt (patient may be unaware), and when looking straight ahead the affected eye appears to deviate upwards and rotate outwards.

title: Friedreich's ataxia – Genetics and epidemiology
content: The most common early-onset hereditary ataxia. Autosomal recessive, trinucleotide repeat disorder (GAA repeat in the X25 gene on chromosome 9, encoding frataxin). Unusual in not demonstrating anticipation. Typical age of onset: 10–15 years. Gait ataxia and kyphoscoliosis are the most common presenting features.

title: Friedreich's ataxia – Clinical features
content: Neurological features: absent ankle jerks/extensor plantars, cerebellar ataxia, optic atrophy, spinocerebellar tract degeneration. Other features: hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (90%, most common cause of death), diabetes mellitus (10–20%), and high-arched palate.

title: Glasgow Coma Scale – Adult scoring
content: Motor response (6): obeys commands (6), localises to pain (5), withdraws from pain (4), abnormal flexion/decorticate (3), extending to pain (2), none (1). Verbal response: orientated (5), confused (4), words (3), sounds (2), none (1). Eye opening: spontaneous (4), to speech (3), to pain (2), none (1). GCS scores expressed as 'GCS = 13, M5 V4 E4 at 21:30'.

title: Guillain-Barré syndrome – Pathogenesis
content: Immune-mediated demyelination of the peripheral nervous system, often triggered by infection (classically Campylobacter jejuni). Cross-reaction of antibodies with gangliosides in the peripheral nervous system. Anti-GM1 antibodies present in 25% of patients. Miller Fisher syndrome variant: ophthalmoplegia, areflexia, and ataxia; descending paralysis; anti-GQ1b antibodies in 90% of cases.

title: Guillain-Barré syndrome – Clinical features
content: Around 65% experience back/leg pain initially. Characteristic feature: progressive, symmetrical ascending weakness (legs first), reduced or absent reflexes, mild sensory symptoms (distal paraesthesia). Other features: respiratory muscle weakness, cranial nerve involvement (diplopia, bilateral facial nerve palsy, oropharyngeal weakness), autonomic involvement (urinary retention, diarrhoea). Less common: papilloedema.

title: Guillain-Barré syndrome – Investigations
content: Lumbar puncture: rise in protein with normal white blood cell count (albuminocytologic dissociation) — found in 66%. Nerve conduction studies: decreased motor nerve conduction velocity (demyelination), prolonged distal motor latency, increased F wave latency.

title: Guillain-Barré syndrome – Management and prognosis
content: IV immunoglobulins (IVIG) or plasma exchange can be used; IVIG is as effective, better tolerated, and easier to administer — generally used first-line. No benefit in combining both. Steroids and immunosuppressants not beneficial. FVC monitoring: >20 mL/kg (usually safe), 15–20 mL/kg (high risk, close monitoring/HDU), <15 mL/kg (impending respiratory failure → ICU), <10 mL/kg (urgent intubation likely). Prognosis: severe motor problems persist in ~15%, ~5% die.

title: Headache – Differential diagnosis by type
content: Migraine: recurrent severe unilateral throbbing headache, may have aura, nausea, photosensitivity, aggravated by routine activities. Tension headache: recurrent non-disabling bilateral 'tight-band' headache, not aggravated by routine activities. Cluster headache: once or twice daily, 15 min–2 hours, intense periorbital pain (always same side), patient restless, redness/lacrimation/lid swelling, more common in men and smokers. Temporal arteritis: >60 years, rapid onset unilateral headache, jaw claudication (65%), tender temporal artery, raised ESR. Medication overuse headache: ≥15 days/month, developed while taking regular symptomatic medication.

title: Headache – Red flags (NICE 2012)
content: Red flag features prompting further action: compromised immunity (HIV/immunosuppression), age <20 years with history of malignancy, known malignancy that metastasises to brain, vomiting without obvious cause, worsening headache with fever, sudden-onset headache reaching maximum intensity within 5 minutes ('thunderclap'), new-onset neurological deficit, new cognitive dysfunction, personality change, impaired consciousness, recent head trauma (within 3 months), headache triggered by cough/Valsalva/sneeze/exercise, orthostatic headache, symptoms of giant cell arteritis or acute narrow-angle glaucoma, substantial change in headache characteristics.

title: Herpes simplex encephalitis – Features and pathophysiology
content: HSV-1 responsible for 95% of adult cases. Characteristically affects temporal and inferior frontal lobes. Features: fever, headache, psychiatric symptoms, seizures, vomiting, focal features (e.g. aphasia). Peripheral lesions (cold sores) have no relation to HSV encephalitis.

title: Herpes simplex encephalitis – Investigations
content: CSF: lymphocytosis, elevated protein. PCR for HSV. CT: medial temporal and inferior frontal changes (petechial haemorrhages) — normal in one-third of patients; MRI is better. EEG: unilateral or bilateral periodic sharp-and-slow-wave complexes at 2–3 Hz over temporal lobes (periodic lateralised epileptiform discharges) — seen in ~80% of cases.

title: Herpes simplex encephalitis – Treatment and prognosis
content: Treatment: intravenous aciclovir. Prognosis depends on early treatment: if started promptly, mortality is 10–20%; untreated, mortality approaches 80%. Complications: cognitive impairment and memory loss (hippocampal damage), personality and behavioural change, seizures/chronic epilepsy, focal neurological deficits, raised ICP/cerebral oedema, Klüver-Bucy syndrome (bilateral temporal lobe involvement — hyperorality, hypersexuality, emotional blunting, docility).

title: HSMN (Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease) – Overview
content: Hereditary sensorimotor neuropathy (HSMN) encompasses Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (also known as peroneal muscular atrophy). Over 7 types have been described. It is the most common inherited peripheral neuropathy.

title: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia – Pathophysiology and features
content: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) results from a lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF), which connects the contralateral CN VI nucleus to the ipsilateral CN III nucleus. Clinical features: impaired adduction of the eye on the same side as the lesion, horizontal nystagmus of the abducting contralateral eye, convergence is preserved. Causes: multiple sclerosis (commonly bilateral MLF lesions), brainstem stroke (typically unilateral, older patients).

title: Lambert-Eaton syndrome – Pathophysiology and features
content: Seen in association with small cell lung cancer (also breast and ovarian cancer) or as an independent autoimmune disorder. Caused by antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels. Features: repeated muscle contractions lead to increased muscle strength (in contrast to myasthenia gravis — seen in only 50% of patients; prolonged use eventually decreases strength), limb-girdle weakness (lower limbs first), hyporeflexia, autonomic symptoms (dry mouth, impotence, difficulty micturating). Ophthalmoplegia and ptosis are not commonly a feature.

title: Lambert-Eaton syndrome – Investigations and management
content: EMG: incremental response to repetitive electrical stimulation. Management: treatment of underlying cancer often leads to significant improvement. Symptomatic treatment: amifampridine (3,4-diaminopyridine) — blocks presynaptic potassium channels, prolongs depolarisation, increases acetylcholine release. Immunomodulatory treatment (if symptoms persist or severe, especially non-paraneoplastic): oral corticosteroids, azathioprine, IVIG, plasma exchange.

title: Lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg's syndrome) – Features
content: Occurs following occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA). Cerebellar features: ataxia and nystagmus. Brainstem features: ipsilateral — dysphagia, facial numbness, cranial nerve palsy (e.g. Horner's syndrome); contralateral — limb sensory loss.

title: Levodopa – Mechanism, use, and adverse effects
content: Levodopa is usually combined with a decarboxylase inhibitor (carbidopa or benserazide) to prevent peripheral metabolism to dopamine. Reduced effectiveness with time (usually by 2 years). No use in neuroleptic-induced parkinsonism. Adverse effects: dyskinesia, 'on-off' effect, postural hypotension, cardiac arrhythmias, nausea and vomiting, psychosis, reddish discolouration of urine upon standing.

title: Median nerve – Anatomy and motor supply
content: The median nerve is formed from lateral (C5–C7) and medial (C8–T1) roots of the brachial plexus. Motor supply in the hand (LOAF): Lateral 2 lumbricals, Opponens pollicis, Abductor pollicis brevis, Flexor pollicis brevis. Sensory: palmar surface of thumb, index, middle, and radial half of ring finger; dorsal surface of distal phalanges of same digits.

title: Median nerve – Patterns of damage
content: Damage at wrist (carpal tunnel syndrome): thenar muscle wasting, loss of thumb opposition (ape thumb deformity), sensory loss over palmar surface of lateral 3½ digits (thenar eminence spared — palmar cutaneous branch). Damage at elbow: all of the above plus inability to pronate forearm, weak wrist flexion with ulnar deviation, impaired flexion of index and middle fingers → hand of benediction when making a fist. Anterior interosseous nerve lesion: weakness of flexor pollicis longus and FDP (index finger) → cannot make 'OK' sign (forms a triangle instead).

title: Medication overuse headache – Features and management
content: One of the most common causes of chronic daily headache, affecting up to 1 in 50 people. Features: present ≥15 days/month, developed or worsened while taking regular symptomatic medication; patients using opioids and triptans are at most risk; may have psychiatric co-morbidity. Management (SIGN 2008): simple analgesics and triptans should be withdrawn abruptly (may initially worsen headaches); opioid analgesics should be gradually withdrawn. Withdrawal symptoms include vomiting, hypotension, tachycardia, restlessness, sleep disturbances, and anxiety.

title: Meningitis – Clinical features and CSF findings
content: Symptoms: headache, fever, nausea/vomiting, photophobia, drowsiness, seizures. Signs: neck stiffness, purpuric rash (especially meningococcal disease). CSF findings: Bacterial — cloudy, low glucose (<1/2 plasma), high protein (>1 g/l), 10–5,000 polymorphs/mm³. Viral — clear/cloudy, 60–80% plasma glucose, normal/raised protein, 15–1,000 lymphocytes/mm³. Tuberculous — slightly cloudy with fibrin web, low glucose, high protein, 10–1,000 lymphocytes/mm³. Ziehl-Neelsen stain only 20% sensitive for TB meningitis; PCR sensitivity 75%.

title: Meningitis – Complications
content: Neurological sequelae: sensorineural hearing loss (most common), seizures, focal neurological deficit. Infective complications: sepsis, intracerebral abscess. Pressure complications: brain herniation, hydrocephalus. Patients with meningococcal meningitis are at risk of Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome (adrenal insufficiency secondary to adrenal haemorrhage).

title: Migraine – Diagnostic criteria (IHS)
content: IHS criteria for migraine without aura: (A) ≥5 attacks fulfilling B–D; (B) attacks lasting 4–72 hours; (C) ≥2 of: unilateral location, pulsating quality, moderate/severe intensity, aggravation by routine physical activity; (D) during headache ≥1 of: nausea/vomiting, photophobia and phonophobia; (E) not attributed to another disorder. Prevalence: 3× more common in women; ~6% in men, ~18% in women.

title: Migraine – Triggers and variants
content: Common triggers: tiredness, stress, alcohol, combined oral contraceptive pill, lack of food or dehydration, cheese/chocolate/red wine/citrus fruits, menstruation, bright lights. Aura: occurs in ~1/3 of patients; typically visual, progressive, lasting 5–60 minutes; transient hemianopic disturbance or spreading scintillating scotoma. Hemiplegic migraine: motor weakness as manifestation of aura; ~50% have strong family history; very rare (estimated prevalence 0.01%).

title: Migraine – Acute treatment with triptans
content: Triptans are specific 5-HT1B and 5-HT1D agonists used first-line in combination with an NSAID or paracetamol. Should be taken as soon as possible after headache onset (not at aura onset). Available as oral, orodispersible, nasal spray, and subcutaneous injection. Adverse effects: 'triptan sensations' — tingling, heat, tightness (throat/chest), heaviness, pressure. Contraindicated in patients with history of or significant risk factors for ischaemic heart disease or cerebrovascular disease.

title: Motor neurone disease – Clinical features
content: Neurological condition of unknown cause presenting with both upper and lower motor neuron signs. Rarely presents before 40 years. Key clues: asymmetric limb weakness (most common presentation of ALS), mixture of LMN and UMN signs, wasting of small hand muscles/tibialis anterior, fasciculations, absence of sensory signs (vague sensory symptoms may occur early but 'never' sensory signs). Does not affect external ocular muscles; no cerebellar signs; sphincter dysfunction is a late feature.

title: Motor neurone disease – Types
content: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (50%): typically LMN signs in arms and UMN signs in legs; familial cases linked to chromosome 21 (superoxide dismutase gene). Primary lateral sclerosis: UMN signs only. Progressive muscular atrophy: LMN signs only, affects distal before proximal muscles, best prognosis. Progressive bulbar palsy: palsy of tongue, chewing/swallowing muscles, and facial muscles due to loss of brainstem motor nuclei; worst prognosis.

title: Motor neurone disease – Management and prognosis
content: Riluzole: prevents stimulation of glutamate receptors; used mainly in ALS; prolongs life by ~3 months. Respiratory care: non-invasive ventilation (usually BiPAP) at night; survival benefit ~7 months. Nutrition: percutaneous gastrostomy tube (PEG) preferred; associated with prolonged survival. Prognosis: poor — 50% of patients die within 3 years.

title: Multiple sclerosis – Epidemiology and subtypes
content: Chronic cell-mediated autoimmune disorder characterised by CNS demyelination. 3× more common in women; most commonly diagnosed aged 20–40 years; 5× more common at higher latitudes. Monozygotic twin concordance 30%, dizygotic 2%. Subtypes: relapsing-remitting (85%, acute attacks followed by remission), secondary progressive (65% of RR patients develop within 15 years, gait and bladder disorders), primary progressive (10%, progressive deterioration from onset, more common in older people).

title: Multiple sclerosis – Clinical features
content: Around 75% of patients have significant lethargy. Visual: optic neuritis (common presenting feature), optic atrophy, Uhthoff's phenomenon (worsening vision with raised body temperature), internuclear ophthalmoplegia. Sensory: pins/needles, numbness, trigeminal neuralgia, Lhermitte's syndrome (paraesthesiae in limbs on neck flexion). Motor: spastic weakness (most commonly legs). Cerebellar: ataxia, tremor. Others: urinary incontinence, sexual dysfunction, intellectual deterioration.

title: Multiple sclerosis – Investigations
content: Diagnosis requires demonstration of lesions disseminated in time and space. MRI: high signal T2 lesions, periventricular plaques, Dawson fingers (hyperintense lesions perpendicular to corpus callosum on FLAIR). CSF: oligoclonal bands (not in serum), increased intrathecal IgG synthesis. Visual evoked potentials: delayed but well-preserved waveform.

title: Multiple sclerosis – Disease-modifying drugs
content: Acute relapse: high-dose steroids (oral or IV methylprednisolone) for 5 days — shortens duration but does not alter degree of recovery. Disease-modifying drugs (typical indications: RR disease + 2 relapses in past 2 years + able to walk 100m unaided; or SP disease + 2 relapses in past 2 years + able to walk 10m): natalizumab (anti-alpha-4-beta-1-integrin, IV, high efficacy, often first-line), ocrelizumab (anti-CD20, IV, high efficacy, often first-line), fingolimod (S1P receptor modulator, oral), beta-interferon (subcutaneous/IM, less effective), glatiramer acetate (immune decoy, subcutaneous).

title: Multiple sclerosis – Symptom management
content: Fatigue: exclude other causes (anaemia, thyroid, depression) then trial amantadine; other options include mindfulness and CBT. Spasticity: baclofen and gabapentin first-line; other options: diazepam, dantrolene, tizanidine; physiotherapy important. Bladder dysfunction: ultrasound to assess emptying first — if significant residual volume → intermittent self-catheterisation; if no significant residual volume → anticholinergics. Oscillopsia: gabapentin first-line.

title: Multiple system atrophy – Features and types
content: Progressive sporadic adult-onset neurodegenerative disorder with autonomic failure, parkinsonism, and cerebellar ataxia. Results from α-synuclein-containing glial cytoplasmic inclusions. MSA-P (Parkinsonian type): predominant extrapyramidal features, poor levodopa response, early autonomic dysfunction. MSA-C (Cerebellar type): predominant cerebellar features (ataxia, dysarthria, gait disturbance), more common in East Asian populations. Features: parkinsonism, erectile dysfunction (often early), postural hypotension, atonic bladder, constipation, anhidrosis, cerebellar signs, pyramidal signs, REM sleep behaviour disorder, stridor.

title: Multiple system atrophy – Investigations and management
content: MRI brain: pontine atrophy ('hot cross bun' sign), putaminal rim hyperintensity, or cerebellar atrophy. Autonomic testing: orthostatic BP drop without compensatory tachycardia. DAT-SPECT: presynaptic dopaminergic deficit similar to Parkinson's disease. Management: symptomatic and supportive (no disease-modifying therapy); trial of levodopa (often limited benefit); fludrocortisone or midodrine for postural hypotension; intermittent catheterisation for urinary dysfunction. Prognosis: median survival 6–10 years after onset.

title: Myasthenia gravis – Pathophysiology and epidemiology
content: Autoimmune disorder with insufficient functioning acetylcholine receptors. Antibodies to acetylcholine receptors in 85–90% of cases. More common in women (2:1). Associated with thymoma (10–15% of patients) and thymic hyperplasia.

title: Narcolepsy – Features and management
content: Narcolepsy is characterised by excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy (sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by emotion — in ~2/3 of patients), sleep paralysis, and hypnagogic hallucinations. Management: daytime stimulants (e.g. modafinil) and nighttime sodium oxybate.

title: Neurofibromatosis – NF1 vs NF2
content: Both autosomal dominant. NF1 (1 in 4,000): mutation in NF1 gene on chromosome 17 → loss of neurofibromin (negative regulator of RAS). Features: ≥6 café-au-lait spots (≥15 mm), axillary/groin freckles, peripheral neurofibromas, Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas, >90%), scoliosis, phaeochromocytomas. NF2 (1 in 100,000): mutation in NF2 gene on chromosome 22 → loss of merlin. Features: bilateral vestibular schwannomas, multiple intracranial schwannomas, meningiomas and ependymomas.

title: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome – Features and management
content: Rare but dangerous condition seen with antipsychotic medication (also atypical antipsychotics and dopaminergic drugs when suddenly stopped). Mortality up to 10%. Occurs within hours to days of starting antipsychotic. Features: pyrexia, muscle rigidity, autonomic lability (hypertension, tachycardia, tachypnoea), agitated delirium. Raised CK in most cases; AKI (rhabdomyolysis) in severe cases; leukocytosis. Management: stop antipsychotic, transfer to medical ward/ICU, IV fluids, dantrolene (decreases excitation-contraction coupling via ryanodine receptor), bromocriptine (dopamine agonist).

title: Neuropathic pain – Definition and management
content: Pain arising following damage or disruption of the nervous system; responds poorly to standard analgesia. Examples: diabetic neuropathy, post-herpetic neuralgia, trigeminal neuralgia, prolapsed intervertebral disc. NICE first-line treatment: amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin, or pregabalin (used as monotherapy — switch rather than add if not working). Tramadol for rescue therapy. Topical capsaicin for localised pain (e.g. post-herpetic neuralgia). Note: carbamazepine is first-line for trigeminal neuralgia.

title: Normal pressure hydrocephalus – Features and management
content: Reversible cause of dementia in elderly patients, secondary to reduced CSF absorption at the arachnoid villi (may follow head injury, subarachnoid haemorrhage, or meningitis). Classical triad: urinary incontinence, dementia and bradyphrenia, gait abnormality (similar to Parkinson's disease). Around 60% have all 3 features at diagnosis. Imaging: hydrocephalus with ventriculomegaly disproportionate to sulcal enlargement. Management: ventriculoperitoneal shunting (~10% experience significant complications including seizures, infection, intracerebral haemorrhage).

title: Parkinson's disease – Features
content: Progressive neurodegenerative condition caused by degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra. Symptoms are characteristically asymmetrical. Classical triad: bradykinesia (poverty of movement, short shuffling steps, reduced arm swing, difficulty initiating movement), tremor (3–5 Hz, most marked at rest, 'pill-rolling', worse when stressed/tired, improves with voluntary movement), rigidity (lead pipe or cogwheel — due to superimposed tremor). Other features: mask-like facies, flexed posture, micrographia, drooling, depression (most common psychiatric feature, ~40%), dementia, psychosis, sleep disturbances, impaired olfaction, REM sleep behaviour disorder, postural hypotension.

title: Parkinson's disease – Management (first-line)
content: NICE 2017 guidelines: if motor symptoms affecting quality of life → levodopa first-line. If motor symptoms not affecting quality of life → dopamine agonist (non-ergot derived), levodopa, or MAO-B inhibitor. Levodopa: more improvement in motor symptoms and ADLs, more motor complications, fewer specified adverse events (excessive sleepiness, hallucinations, impulse control disorders). Dopamine agonists and MAO-B inhibitors: less motor improvement but fewer motor complications, more specified adverse events.

title: Parkinson's disease – Adjunct therapy and impulse control
content: If symptoms persist despite optimal levodopa or dyskinesia develops, add dopamine agonist, MAO-B inhibitor, or COMT inhibitor. COMT inhibitors: more adverse events, more off-time reduction. Amantadine: no evidence for motor symptoms or ADLs. Impulse control disorders: more common with dopamine agonists, history of impulsive behaviour, alcohol, or smoking. Dopamine dysregulation syndrome: compulsive overuse of dopaminergic medication (especially levodopa), drug-seeking behaviour despite worsening dyskinesia.

title: Parkinson's disease – Specific medication management
content: Risk of acute akinesia or NMS if medication not taken/absorbed (e.g. gastroenteritis) — avoid 'drug holidays'. Excessive daytime sleepiness: adjust medication; consider modafinil if other strategies fail; patient should not drive. Orthostatic hypotension: medication review; if persists → midodrine (peripheral alpha-adrenergic agonist). Drooling: consider glycopyrronium bromide.

title: Pituitary apoplexy – Phenytoin adverse effects (duplicate entry note)
content: Pituitary apoplexy is a clinical syndrome caused by haemorrhage or infarction of the pituitary gland, often in the context of a pre-existing pituitary adenoma. It presents with sudden severe headache, visual disturbances (including bitemporal hemianopia), ophthalmoplegia, and features of hypopituitarism. It is a neurosurgical emergency.

title: Post-lumbar puncture headache – Features and management
content: Occurs in ~1/3 of patients. Typically develops within 24–48 hours (up to 1 week). Worsens with upright position, improves with recumbent position. Risk increased by: conventional 'cutting' needles (vs pencil-point atraumatic needles), larger needle size, incorrect bevel direction, not replacing the stylet, increased LP attempts. Management: supportive initially (analgesia, rest). If pain continues >72 hours: blood patch, epidural saline, or IV caffeine (to prevent subdural haematoma).

title: Progressive supranuclear palsy – Features and investigations
content: Also known as Steele-Richardson-Olszewski syndrome; a 'Parkinson Plus' syndrome. Features: postural instability and falls, stiff broad-based gait, impairment of vertical gaze (down gaze worse than up gaze — difficulty reading or descending stairs), parkinsonism with prominent bradykinesia, cognitive impairment (primarily frontal lobe dysfunction). MRI: midbrain atrophy with relative preservation of pons, 'hummingbird sign' (sagittal view), dilated third ventricle. DAT scan: may show reduced uptake but does not reliably distinguish from Parkinson's disease. Management: poor response to L-dopa.

title: Psychogenic non-epileptic seizures – Distinguishing features
content: Factors favouring psychogenic non-epileptic seizures (pseudoseizures): pelvic thrusting, family member with epilepsy, much more common in females, crying after seizure, don't occur when alone, gradual onset. Factors favouring true epileptic seizures: tongue biting, raised serum prolactin (thought to result from spread of electrical activity to ventromedial hypothalamus). Video telemetry is useful for differentiating.

title: Radial nerve – Anatomy and patterns of damage
content: Continuation of posterior cord of brachial plexus (C5–T1). Spirals around posterior surface of humerus in the radial groove. Motor (main nerve): triceps, anconeus, brachioradialis, extensor carpi radialis. Motor (posterior interosseous branch): supinator, extensor carpi ulnaris, extensor digitorum, extensor indicis, extensor digiti minimi, extensor pollicis longus and brevis, abductor pollicis longus. Damage: wrist drop, sensory loss over small area between dorsal 1st and 2nd metacarpals. Axillary damage: additionally paralysis of triceps.

title: Raised intracranial pressure – Pathophysiology, causes, and features
content: Normal ICP: 7–15 mmHg in adults (supine). CPP = MAP − ICP. Causes: idiopathic intracranial hypertension, traumatic head injuries, infection (meningitis), tumours, hydrocephalus. Features: headache, vomiting, reduced consciousness, papilloedema, Cushing's triad (widening pulse pressure, bradycardia, irregular breathing). ICP monitoring: catheter in lateral ventricles; cut-off >20 mmHg for further treatment.

title: Raised intracranial pressure – Management
content: Investigate and treat underlying cause. Head elevation to 30°. IV mannitol (osmotic diuretic). Controlled hyperventilation: reduce pCO2 → cerebral vasoconstriction → reduced ICP (rapid but temporary; caution as may reduce blood flow to ischaemic areas). CSF removal: drain from intraventricular monitor, repeated lumbar puncture (idiopathic intracranial hypertension), or ventriculoperitoneal shunt (hydrocephalus).

title: Reflexes – Root values
content: Common reflex root values: Ankle — S1–S2. Knee — L3–L4. Biceps — C5–C6. Triceps — C7–C8.

title: Restless legs syndrome – Features, causes, and management
content: Affects 2–10% of the general population; males and females equally affected. Features: uncontrollable urge to move legs (akathisia), worse at rest, initially nocturnal; paraesthesias ('crawling' or 'throbbing'); periodic limb movements of sleep (PLMS). Causes/associations: positive family history in 50% of idiopathic cases, iron deficiency anaemia, uraemia, diabetes mellitus, pregnancy. Management: simple measures (walking, stretching, massage), treat iron deficiency. First-line: alpha-2-delta ligands (pregabalin or gabapentin) — preferred over dopamine agonists due to high rates of augmentation and impulse control disorders.

title: Reye's syndrome – Features and management
content: Severe progressive encephalopathy affecting children, accompanied by fatty infiltration of the liver, kidneys, and pancreas. Associated with aspirin use and a viral cause. Peak incidence at 2 years of age. Features: preceding viral illness, encephalopathy (confusion, seizures, cerebral oedema, coma), fatty infiltration of liver/kidneys/pancreas, hypoglycaemia. Management: supportive. Mortality: 15–25%.

title: Sixth nerve palsy – Causes and features
content: The abducens nerve (CN VI) supplies the lateral rectus muscle. Palsy features: horizontal diplopia (worse on looking towards affected side), eye deviated medially at rest, inability to abduct the eye. Causes: raised intracranial pressure (false localising sign — stretched over petrous temporal bone), microvascular disease (diabetes, hypertension), trauma, demyelination, tumours, Wernicke's encephalopathy, meningitis.

title: Spinal cord compression – Causes and clinical features
content: Causes: metastatic tumour (most common — breast, lung, prostate, kidney, myeloma), disc prolapse, epidural abscess, haematoma. Features: bilateral limb weakness (UMN signs below level), sensory level, bladder dysfunction (urinary retention early, incontinence late), bowel dysfunction, back pain (often worse lying flat). Cauda equina syndrome: compression below L1 — LMN signs, saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention/overflow incontinence, faecal incontinence, reduced anal tone.

title: Spinal cord compression – Management
content: Urgent MRI spine (whole spine if malignancy suspected). Dexamethasone immediately (reduces oedema). Neurosurgical or orthopaedic referral. Radiotherapy for radiosensitive tumours. Surgical decompression if: uncertain diagnosis, spinal instability, radioresistant tumour, previous maximum radiotherapy, neurological deterioration during radiotherapy. Cauda equina: surgical emergency — urgent decompression within 24 hours.

title: Spinal cord injury – Incomplete cord syndromes
content: Central cord syndrome: most common incomplete injury; hyperextension in older patients with cervical spondylosis; disproportionate weakness in arms > legs, bladder dysfunction, variable sensory loss. Anterior cord syndrome: anterior spinal artery occlusion; bilateral loss of motor function and pain/temperature below lesion; preserved vibration and proprioception (posterior columns intact). Brown-Séquard syndrome: hemisection; ipsilateral loss of motor function, vibration, and proprioception; contralateral loss of pain and temperature (spinothalamic tract crosses 1–2 levels above).

title: Spinal cord injury – Acute management
content: Immobilise spine. Methylprednisolone: no longer routinely recommended (CRASH trial — increased mortality and infection). Surgical decompression and stabilisation. Neuroprotective strategies under investigation. Complications: neurogenic shock (hypotension + bradycardia — loss of sympathetic tone), spinal shock (flaccid paralysis initially, then spasticity), autonomic dysreflexia (SCI above T6 — severe hypertension, bradycardia, headache, sweating triggered by noxious stimulus below lesion), pressure sores, DVT/PE, UTI.

title: Stroke – Pathophysiology and classification
content: Ischaemic stroke (85%): thrombotic (atherosclerosis of large or small vessels) or embolic (cardiac — AF, valvular disease; arterial — carotid atherosclerosis). Haemorrhagic stroke (15%): intracerebral haemorrhage (hypertension most common cause) or subarachnoid haemorrhage. TOAST classification of ischaemic stroke: large artery atherosclerosis, cardioembolism, small artery occlusion (lacunar), other determined aetiology, undetermined aetiology.

title: Stroke – Clinical features by territory
content: Anterior circulation (MCA/ACA): contralateral hemiplegia (face and arm > leg in MCA; leg > arm in ACA), contralateral hemisensory loss, homonymous hemianopia, dysphasia (dominant hemisphere), neglect (non-dominant hemisphere). Posterior circulation (PCA/basilar/vertebral): diplopia, vertigo, ataxia, nystagmus, dysphagia, dysarthria, crossed sensory/motor deficits. Lacunar infarcts: pure motor, pure sensory, sensorimotor, ataxic hemiparesis, dysarthria-clumsy hand.

title: Stroke – Acute management (ischaemic)
content: Thrombolysis (alteplase): within 4.5 hours of onset if no contraindications; CT head first to exclude haemorrhage. Mechanical thrombectomy: large vessel occlusion (ICA, M1/M2 MCA, basilar); within 24 hours; combined with thrombolysis if eligible. Aspirin 300 mg: if thrombolysis not given, start within 24 hours; continue for 2 weeks then switch to clopidogrel. Blood pressure: do not lower acutely unless hypertensive emergency or thrombolysis planned (target <185/110 mmHg). Swallowing assessment before oral intake.

title: Stroke – Secondary prevention
content: Antiplatelet therapy: clopidogrel 75 mg daily (first-line); aspirin + dipyridamole MR if clopidogrel not tolerated. Anticoagulation: if AF present — start after 2 weeks (or immediately if TIA/minor stroke). Statin therapy: atorvastatin 80 mg. Blood pressure control: target <130/80 mmHg. Lifestyle: smoking cessation, diet, exercise, alcohol moderation. Carotid endarterectomy: if 50–99% symptomatic stenosis — within 2 weeks of TIA/minor stroke.

title: Subarachnoid haemorrhage – Causes and clinical features
content: 85% due to rupture of berry aneurysm (associated with ADPKD, Ehlers-Danlos, Marfan's, coarctation of the aorta). Other causes: AVM, trauma. Features: sudden-onset 'thunderclap' headache (worst headache of life, reaching maximum intensity within seconds to minutes), vomiting, neck stiffness (may take hours to develop), photophobia, loss of consciousness, focal neurological deficit. Sentinel headache: warning headache days/weeks before major bleed (occurs in ~20% of cases).

title: Subarachnoid haemorrhage – Investigations and management
content: CT head (non-contrast): hyperdense blood in subarachnoid space; sensitivity ~98% within 6 hours of onset, falls to ~50% at 1 week. LP: if CT negative and >6 hours from onset — xanthochromia (yellow discolouration of CSF due to haemoglobin breakdown products, detected by spectrophotometry). Management: neurosurgical referral, nimodipine (calcium channel blocker — reduces vasospasm and improves outcome), aneurysm treatment (coiling preferred over clipping). Complications: rebleeding (highest risk in first 24 hours), vasospasm (days 4–14), hydrocephalus, hyponatraemia (SIADH or cerebral salt wasting).

title: Subdural haemorrhage – Types and clinical features
content: Acute subdural haematoma: high-energy trauma, often with underlying brain injury; bridging veins torn; blood accumulates rapidly; presents with rapid deterioration. Chronic subdural haematoma: elderly/alcoholic patients, minor or no trauma, slow accumulation over weeks; presents with fluctuating consciousness, headache, cognitive decline, focal neurological deficit. CT head: hyperdense (acute) or hypodense (chronic) crescent-shaped collection crossing suture lines, midline shift.

title: Subdural haemorrhage – Management
content: Acute: neurosurgical emergency — craniotomy and evacuation. Chronic: if symptomatic or significant midline shift → burr hole drainage; if asymptomatic and small → conservative management with serial imaging. Anticoagulants should be reversed. Avoid antiplatelet agents. Seizure prophylaxis may be considered.

title: Extradural haemorrhage – Features and management
content: Typically follows temporal bone fracture rupturing the middle meningeal artery. Biconvex (lenticular) hyperdense collection on CT, does not cross suture lines. Classic history: initial loss of consciousness, then lucid interval, then rapid deterioration (herniation). Management: urgent neurosurgical evacuation. Prognosis: excellent if treated promptly.

title: Syncope – Causes and clinical differentiation
content: Vasovagal syncope: most common; precipitated by prolonged standing, heat, pain, emotion; prodrome (nausea, pallor, sweating), brief loss of consciousness, rapid recovery. Cardiac syncope: sudden onset without prodrome, may occur during exertion; associated with palpitations, chest pain; ECG abnormalities. Orthostatic hypotension: on standing, BP drop >20 mmHg systolic or >10 mmHg diastolic within 3 minutes. Carotid sinus hypersensitivity: triggered by head turning, tight collar. Seizures: tongue biting, post-ictal confusion, incontinence, prolonged recovery.

title: Temporal arteritis – Features and management
content: Also known as giant cell arteritis (GCA). Affects patients >50 years (peak 70–80 years). Features: severe unilateral temporal headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication (65%), tender/thickened/nodular temporal artery, visual loss (ischaemic optic neuropathy — most feared complication), polymyalgia rheumatica (50%). ESR >50 mm/hr (often >100), CRP elevated. Temporal artery biopsy: gold standard but skip lesions may give false negative. Management: high-dose prednisolone immediately (do not wait for biopsy) — 40–60 mg/day (60 mg if visual symptoms). Tocilizumab (IL-6 receptor antagonist) for relapsing/refractory disease.

title: Third nerve palsy – Causes and features
content: CN III supplies superior rectus, inferior rectus, medial rectus, inferior oblique (eye movements), levator palpebrae (lid elevation), and pupillary constrictor. Complete palsy: ptosis, eye deviated 'down and out', fixed dilated pupil (if pupil-involving). Pupil-involving causes: posterior communicating artery aneurysm (surgical emergency — compresses parasympathetic fibres on outside of nerve), uncal herniation. Pupil-sparing causes: microvascular disease (diabetes, hypertension — ischaemia of central nerve fibres, parasympathetic fibres on outside spared).

title: Transient ischaemic attack – Definition and assessment
content: Transient neurological dysfunction due to focal brain, spinal cord, or retinal ischaemia, without acute infarction, typically lasting <24 hours (usually <1 hour). ABCD2 score (risk of stroke within 2 days): Age ≥60 (1), Blood pressure ≥140/90 (1), Clinical features — unilateral weakness (2), speech disturbance without weakness (1), Duration ≥60 min (2), 10–59 min (1), Diabetes (1). High risk (score ≥4): specialist assessment within 24 hours. Low risk (score <4): within 1 week.

title: Trigeminal neuralgia – Features and management
content: Severe paroxysmal unilateral facial pain in the distribution of CN V (most commonly V2 or V3). Described as electric shock-like or stabbing. Triggered by light touch (eating, talking, brushing teeth). Secondary causes: multiple sclerosis, compression by blood vessel (most common structural cause). Management: carbamazepine first-line (70–80% response). Alternatives: oxcarbazepine, lamotrigine, gabapentin. Surgical options (for refractory cases): microvascular decompression (Jannetta procedure), percutaneous rhizotomy, stereotactic radiosurgery (Gamma Knife).

title: Ulnar nerve – Anatomy and patterns of damage
content: Formed from medial cord of brachial plexus (C8–T1). Motor: flexor carpi ulnaris, medial half of FDP, hypothenar muscles, all interossei, medial 2 lumbricals, adductor pollicis, palmaris brevis. Sensory: little finger, medial half of ring finger, medial palm. Damage at wrist: 'claw hand' (ring and little fingers — hyperextension at MCP, flexion at IP joints), wasting of hypothenar and interossei, loss of finger abduction/adduction, Froment's sign (flexion of thumb IP joint when gripping paper — adductor pollicis weakness). Damage at elbow: all of above plus loss of wrist flexion with radial deviation, loss of FDP to ring/little fingers.

title: Vertigo – Causes and clinical differentiation
content: Peripheral causes (more common): BPPV (most common — brief episodes triggered by head movement, positive Dix-Hallpike test, Epley manoeuvre treatment), Ménière's disease (episodic vertigo + tinnitus + hearing loss + aural fullness), vestibular neuritis (acute severe vertigo without hearing loss, follows viral URTI, lasts days to weeks), labyrinthitis (vertigo + hearing loss). Central causes (less common but more serious): cerebellar stroke/haemorrhage, brainstem lesion, MS, acoustic neuroma. Red flags: sudden onset, headache, diplopia, dysphagia, dysarthria, ataxia, new hearing loss.

title: Wernicke's encephalopathy – Pathophysiology and features
content: Caused by thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, most commonly in alcohol dependence but also in malnutrition, prolonged vomiting, eating disorders, bariatric surgery. Pathology: haemorrhagic lesions in periventricular grey matter, mammillary bodies, thalamus. Classical triad (all 3 present in only 10%): confusion/encephalopathy, ophthalmoplegia (bilateral CN VI palsy most common, nystagmus), ataxia. If untreated → Korsakoff's syndrome: anterograde and retrograde amnesia, confabulation, relatively preserved consciousness.

title: Wernicke's encephalopathy – Management
content: IV thiamine (Pabrinex) is the treatment of choice — must be given before glucose (glucose infusion can precipitate or worsen Wernicke's). Give high-dose IV thiamine (Pabrinex 2 pairs of ampoules TDS for 3–5 days) in suspected cases. Oral thiamine is insufficient for acute treatment. Prophylactic thiamine should be given to all patients with alcohol dependence.

title: Dementia – Types and distinguishing features
content: Alzheimer's disease (most common, ~60%): insidious onset, progressive memory loss, visuospatial difficulties, language problems; pathology — amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles. Vascular dementia (~20%): stepwise deterioration, focal neurological signs, cardiovascular risk factors. Lewy body dementia (~15%): fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, REM sleep behaviour disorder, sensitivity to antipsychotics. Frontotemporal dementia: personality/behavioural change, executive dysfunction, language problems, relatively preserved memory early.

title: Dementia – Investigations
content: Bloods: FBC, U&E, LFTs, TFTs, glucose, B12/folate, calcium, lipids, syphilis serology (if risk factors). Urine: MSU. Imaging: CT or MRI head (to exclude reversible causes, identify type). EEG: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (periodic sharp wave complexes). CSF: 14-3-3 protein (CJD), amyloid/tau ratio (Alzheimer's). SPECT/PET: dopamine transporter scan (DaTscan) for Lewy body dementia. Neuropsychological testing: MMSE, MoCA, ACE-III.

title: Dementia – Management
content: Alzheimer's disease: acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) for mild-moderate disease; memantine (NMDA receptor antagonist) for moderate-severe disease or if AChEI not tolerated. Vascular dementia: optimise cardiovascular risk factors; no specific licensed treatment. Lewy body dementia: AChEI (rivastigmine has most evidence); avoid antipsychotics (risk of severe neuroleptic sensitivity reaction). Behavioural and psychological symptoms: non-pharmacological first-line; antipsychotics only if severe distress/risk (use with caution, especially in Lewy body).

title: Diabetic neuropathy – Types and features
content: Peripheral neuropathy: most common; symmetrical, length-dependent, sensorimotor; glove and stocking distribution; burning, tingling, numbness; loss of vibration and proprioception first (large fibres), then pain and temperature (small fibres). Autonomic neuropathy: postural hypotension, gastroparesis, diarrhoea, erectile dysfunction, bladder dysfunction, anhidrosis. Mononeuropathy: sudden onset, single nerve (e.g. CN III palsy — pupil-sparing, painful); usually self-limiting. Amyotrophy (diabetic lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy): severe asymmetric proximal leg weakness and pain.

title: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension – Features and management
content: Also known as pseudotumour cerebri or benign intracranial hypertension. Predominantly affects obese women of childbearing age. Associations: obesity, tetracyclines, vitamin A excess, oral contraceptive pill, steroids (withdrawal), lithium. Features: headache (worse in morning, on lying down, on Valsalva), pulsatile tinnitus, visual obscurations, papilloedema, CN VI palsy (false localising sign). Visual field testing: enlarged blind spot, peripheral constriction. Management: weight loss (most important), acetazolamide (carbonic anhydrase inhibitor), topiramate; repeated LP; optic nerve sheath fenestration or CSF shunting if vision threatened.
