title: Carpal tunnel syndrome – Features and management
content: Compression of the median nerve at the wrist within the carpal tunnel. Associations: pregnancy, hypothyroidism, rheumatoid arthritis, diabetes, acromegaly, obesity. Features: pain and paraesthesia in median nerve distribution (thumb, index, middle, radial half of ring finger), worse at night, relieved by shaking hand (flick test). Signs: Tinel's test (tapping over carpal tunnel), Phalen's test (wrist flexion for 60 seconds). Investigations: nerve conduction studies. Management: wrist splints (especially at night), steroid injection, surgical decompression.

title: Myasthenia gravis – Clinical features
content: Fatigable weakness: worsens with repeated use, improves with rest. Ocular features (most common presentation): ptosis (often asymmetric, worsens with sustained upgaze), diplopia. Bulbar features: dysarthria, dysphagia, nasal regurgitation. Limb weakness: proximal > distal. Myasthenic crisis: severe respiratory muscle weakness requiring ventilation — precipitated by infection, surgery, medication changes.

title: Myasthenia gravis – Investigations and management
content: Investigations: anti-AChR antibodies (85–90%), anti-MuSK antibodies (if AChR negative), CT chest (thymoma), single-fibre EMG (most sensitive), Tensilon (edrophonium) test (rarely used now — cholinergic crisis risk). Management: pyridostigmine (acetylcholinesterase inhibitor — symptomatic treatment); immunosuppression (prednisolone, azathioprine); thymectomy (if thymoma or generalised disease in patients <60 years); IVIG or plasma exchange for crisis.

title: Cerebral palsy – Types and features
content: Non-progressive disorder of posture and movement due to damage to the developing brain (before, during, or after birth). Spastic (most common, ~70–80%): UMN signs, increased tone, hyperreflexia; hemiplegia, diplegia, or quadriplegia. Dyskinetic/athetoid (~10–15%): involuntary writhing movements, fluctuating tone, often due to kernicterus or hypoxia. Ataxic (~5%): cerebellar signs, hypotonia, unsteady gait. Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy: perinatal asphyxia → periventricular leukomalacia (premature infants) or basal ganglia/cortical injury (term infants).

title: Cerebral palsy – Management
content: Multidisciplinary approach. Spasticity: physiotherapy, baclofen (oral or intrathecal), botulinum toxin injections, orthopaedic surgery. Seizures: antiepileptic drugs. Communication: speech and language therapy, augmentative communication devices. Nutrition: gastrostomy feeding if dysphagia. Educational support. Associated conditions: intellectual disability, epilepsy, visual/hearing impairment, behavioural problems.

title: Muscular dystrophies – Duchenne and Becker
content: Duchenne muscular dystrophy: X-linked recessive, dystrophin gene mutation (frameshift → absent dystrophin), 1 in 3,500 male births. Onset: 3–5 years, proximal muscle weakness (Gowers' sign), pseudohypertrophy of calves, cardiomyopathy, respiratory failure. Raised CK. Becker muscular dystrophy: X-linked recessive, dystrophin gene mutation (in-frame → reduced/abnormal dystrophin), later onset (5–15 years), milder course, cardiomyopathy prominent. Management: corticosteroids (deflazacort/prednisolone) delay progression; ataluren (for nonsense mutations); supportive care.

title: Muscular dystrophies – Myotonic dystrophy
content: Most common adult muscular dystrophy. Autosomal dominant, CTG repeat expansion in DMPK gene (chromosome 19). Anticipation: worsens with successive generations. Features: myotonia (inability to relax muscles after contraction — grip myotonia, percussion myotonia), distal muscle weakness (unusual for muscular dystrophy), ptosis, cataracts, frontal baldness, cardiomyopathy/arrhythmias, intellectual impairment, diabetes, testicular atrophy. Congenital form: severe hypotonia, respiratory failure, intellectual disability.

title: Radiculopathy – Cervical and lumbar features
content: Cervical radiculopathy: C5 (shoulder/upper arm pain, deltoid/biceps weakness, reduced biceps reflex), C6 (lateral forearm/thumb pain, biceps/brachioradialis weakness, reduced biceps/supinator reflex), C7 (posterior arm/middle finger pain, triceps/wrist extensor weakness, reduced triceps reflex), C8 (medial forearm/little finger pain, finger flexor/intrinsic hand muscle weakness). Lumbar radiculopathy: L4 (medial leg/foot pain, quadriceps weakness, reduced knee reflex), L5 (lateral leg/dorsal foot pain, foot/great toe dorsiflexion weakness, no reflex change), S1 (posterior leg/lateral foot pain, plantarflexion weakness, reduced ankle reflex).

title: Radiculopathy – Management
content: Conservative management (most cases): analgesia (NSAIDs, neuropathic agents), physiotherapy, activity modification. Indications for urgent imaging and surgical referral: progressive neurological deficit, cauda equina syndrome, myelopathy, cancer or infection suspected. MRI spine: investigation of choice. Surgical options: discectomy (disc prolapse), laminectomy (spinal stenosis), foraminotomy (foraminal stenosis). Epidural steroid injections: short-term pain relief.

title: Brain metastases – Features and management
content: Most common intracranial tumour in adults. Common primary sources: lung (most common), breast, melanoma, renal, colorectal. Features: headache (worse in morning, on Valsalva), focal neurological deficit, seizures, cognitive decline, raised ICP. CT/MRI: multiple ring-enhancing lesions with surrounding oedema. Management: dexamethasone (reduces oedema), whole brain radiotherapy (palliative), stereotactic radiosurgery (limited number of metastases), surgical resection (single accessible metastasis with controlled primary), systemic therapy (targeted/immunotherapy for certain primaries).

title: Brain abscess – Features and management
content: Focal collection of pus within the brain parenchyma. Sources: haematogenous spread (lung abscess, infective endocarditis, dental sepsis), direct spread (sinusitis, otitis media, mastoiditis), trauma/surgery. Common organisms: Streptococcus (most common), Staphylococcus, anaerobes, Gram-negative bacilli. Features: headache, fever (only 50%), focal neurological deficit, seizures, raised ICP. CT/MRI: ring-enhancing lesion with surrounding oedema. Management: IV antibiotics (cefotaxime + metronidazole), neurosurgical drainage (stereotactic aspiration or excision), dexamethasone (controversial).

title: Acoustic neuroma – Features and management
content: Benign schwannoma of the vestibular branch of CN VIII. Most common cerebellopontine angle tumour. Bilateral in NF2. Features: unilateral sensorineural hearing loss (most common presenting symptom), tinnitus, vertigo/dysequilibrium, facial numbness (CN V involvement), facial weakness (CN VII — late feature), cerebellar signs (large tumours). Investigations: MRI internal auditory meatus (gadolinium-enhanced), pure tone audiogram. Management: observation (small tumours), stereotactic radiosurgery (Gamma Knife), surgical resection (translabyrinthine, retrosigmoid, or middle fossa approach).

title: Ménière's disease – Features and management
content: Disorder of the inner ear characterised by excess endolymph (endolymphatic hydrops). Features: episodic vertigo (lasting 20 minutes to 24 hours), fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss (low frequencies initially), tinnitus, aural fullness. Diagnosis: clinical. Investigations: pure tone audiogram, MRI (to exclude other pathology). Management: acute attacks — prochlorperazine or cinnarizine (vestibular sedatives); long-term — low-salt diet, betahistine (increases cochlear blood flow), thiazide diuretics; surgical options for refractory cases (endolymphatic sac decompression, intratympanic gentamicin, labyrinthectomy).

title: Essential tremor – Features and management
content: Most common movement disorder. Autosomal dominant in 50% of cases. Features: bilateral postural/action tremor (hands most commonly affected), absent at rest, may affect head (titubation), voice, and legs; relieved by alcohol. Worsened by caffeine, stress, fatigue. Investigations: clinical diagnosis; DaTscan normal (distinguishes from Parkinson's disease). Management: propranolol (first-line), primidone (first-line alternative); topiramate, gabapentin (second-line); deep brain stimulation (DBS) for severe refractory cases.

title: Chronic fatigue syndrome – Diagnostic criteria and management
content: Also known as myalgic encephalomyelitis (ME/CFS). NICE 2021 diagnostic criteria: debilitating fatigue (worsened by activity), post-exertional malaise (PEM — worsening of symptoms after physical, cognitive, or emotional exertion), unrefreshing sleep, cognitive impairment ('brain fog'); plus one of: orthostatic intolerance or pain. Symptoms present ≥3 months. Management: energy management/pacing (avoid boom-bust cycles), sleep management, cognitive rehabilitation therapy; NICE 2021 no longer recommends graded exercise therapy (GET) or CBT as curative treatments.

title: Driving and neurological conditions – DVLA guidance
content: Epilepsy: must not drive for 1 year after a seizure (Group 1 — car/motorcycle); 5 years seizure-free for Group 2 (HGV/bus). Blackouts/syncope: must stop driving if unexplained loss of consciousness; may resume after 4 weeks if cause identified and treated (Group 1). TIA/stroke: must not drive for 1 month (Group 1); 1 year for Group 2. Parkinson's disease: must notify DVLA; driving may continue if condition is controlled. Dementia: must notify DVLA; assessed individually. Narcolepsy: must not drive until symptoms controlled.

title: Spinal fracture – Types and management
content: Mechanism: trauma (flexion-compression, extension, rotation), pathological (osteoporosis, malignancy). Stable fractures: do not compromise spinal cord; managed conservatively (analgesia, bracing). Unstable fractures: risk of spinal cord injury; require surgical stabilisation. Burst fractures: high-energy axial loading, vertebral body comminution, retropulsion of fragments into canal. Chance fractures: flexion-distraction injury (seatbelt injury), horizontal fracture through vertebra. Osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures: most common in elderly; managed with analgesia, bisphosphonates, vertebroplasty/kyphoplasty for refractory pain.

title: Bell's palsy – Features and management
content: Idiopathic lower motor neuron facial nerve (CN VII) palsy. Thought to be due to herpes simplex virus reactivation. Features: unilateral facial weakness (forehead involved — distinguishes from UMN lesion), inability to close eye (lagophthalmos), loss of nasolabial fold, drooping of mouth, loss of taste (anterior 2/3 of tongue), hyperacusis, reduced lacrimation. Management: prednisolone (within 72 hours of onset — improves recovery), eye protection (lubricating drops, tape eye shut at night), antivirals (aciclovir — added benefit uncertain). Prognosis: ~85% fully recover within 3 months.

title: Malaria – Cerebral malaria features
content: Cerebral malaria is the most severe neurological complication of Plasmodium falciparum infection. Features: fever, impaired consciousness (coma), seizures, focal neurological deficits, retinal haemorrhages. Pathophysiology: sequestration of parasitised red blood cells in cerebral microvasculature, cytokine-mediated inflammation, hypoglycaemia. Management: IV artesunate (first-line), IV quinine (if artesunate unavailable); dexamethasone not recommended (increases coma duration); treat hypoglycaemia; anticonvulsants for seizures.

title: Optic neuritis – Features and management
content: Inflammation of the optic nerve, most commonly associated with multiple sclerosis (first presentation in ~25% of MS patients). Features: painful loss of vision (pain worse with eye movement), reduced visual acuity, colour desaturation (red desaturation), central scotoma, relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD — Marcus Gunn pupil), Uhthoff's phenomenon (worsening with heat/exercise). Fundoscopy: optic disc swelling (if anterior) or normal (retrobulbar neuritis). Management: IV methylprednisolone (speeds recovery but does not improve final visual acuity); MRI brain to assess MS risk.

title: Horner's syndrome – Causes and features
content: Interruption of the sympathetic supply to the eye. Features: partial ptosis (superior tarsal muscle), miosis (pupil constriction), anhidrosis (loss of sweating — if lesion is below superior cervical ganglion), enophthalmos (apparent). Causes by level: central (hypothalamus to ciliospinal centre of Budge, C8–T2): stroke, MS, syringomyelia, tumour; preganglionic (C8–T2 to superior cervical ganglion): Pancoast tumour, cervical rib, thyroid carcinoma, lymphadenopathy; postganglionic (superior cervical ganglion to eye): carotid artery dissection (painful Horner's), cavernous sinus thrombosis, cluster headache.

title: Cluster headache – Features and management
content: Severe unilateral periorbital pain, lasting 15 minutes to 3 hours, occurring in clusters (1–8 attacks per day for weeks to months, then remission). More common in men (3:1), typically 20–40 years, strong association with smoking. Features: ipsilateral autonomic features (lacrimation, rhinorrhoea, conjunctival injection, ptosis, miosis, eyelid oedema), patient is restless (unlike migraine). Acute treatment: 100% oxygen (10–15 L/min for 15 minutes), subcutaneous sumatriptan. Prophylaxis: verapamil (first-line), lithium, topiramate, short course prednisolone (for rapid relief while verapamil takes effect).

title: Migraine – Prophylaxis
content: NICE recommends prophylaxis if ≥4 attacks per month or attacks are particularly disabling. First-line: topiramate (teratogenic — avoid in women of childbearing age without contraception), propranolol. Second-line: amitriptyline, sodium valproate (teratogenic), gabapentin. CGRP monoclonal antibodies (erenumab, fremanezumab, galcanezumab): for chronic migraine or episodic migraine failing 3 previous preventive treatments. Botulinum toxin type A: for chronic migraine (≥15 headache days/month, ≥8 of which are migraine).

title: Lumbar puncture – Indications and contraindications
content: Indications: suspected meningitis/encephalitis, subarachnoid haemorrhage (if CT negative), idiopathic intracranial hypertension, MS (oligoclonal bands), Guillain-Barré syndrome, cryptococcal meningitis. Contraindications: raised ICP with risk of coning (papilloedema, focal neurological signs, altered consciousness → CT first), coagulopathy (INR >1.5, platelets <50), local infection at site, suspected spinal cord compression. Complications: post-LP headache (most common), infection, haematoma, nerve root damage, coning (if raised ICP not excluded).

title: Meningitis – Management
content: Bacterial meningitis: do not delay antibiotics for CT or LP. IV ceftriaxone (or cefotaxime) immediately. Add ampicillin/amoxicillin if Listeria suspected (age >55, immunocompromised, pregnancy). Dexamethasone: reduces complications (especially hearing loss in pneumococcal meningitis) — give with or before first antibiotic dose. Viral meningitis: supportive management; IV aciclovir if HSV suspected. Meningococcal disease: IM benzylpenicillin in community before transfer. Prophylaxis: ciprofloxacin or rifampicin for close contacts of meningococcal disease.

title: Peripheral neuropathy – Classification and causes
content: By fibre type: large fibre (vibration, proprioception, motor — e.g. B12 deficiency, HSMN), small fibre (pain, temperature — e.g. diabetes, amyloid). By pattern: mononeuropathy (single nerve — diabetes, trauma, entrapment), mononeuritis multiplex (multiple non-contiguous nerves — vasculitis, diabetes, leprosy, sarcoidosis), polyneuropathy (symmetric, length-dependent — metabolic, toxic, hereditary). Common causes: diabetes (most common in UK), alcohol, B12 deficiency, hypothyroidism, uraemia, paraproteinaemia, paraneoplastic, drugs (isoniazid, vincristine, metronidazole, amiodarone), hereditary (HSMN).

title: Head injury – Assessment and management
content: NICE CT head criteria (adults): GCS <13 on initial assessment, GCS <15 at 2 hours, suspected open/depressed skull fracture, any sign of basal skull fracture (haemotympanum, 'panda eyes', cerebrospinal fluid leakage, Battle's sign), post-traumatic seizure, focal neurological deficit, >1 episode of vomiting, age ≥65 with amnesia or loss of consciousness. Management: ABCDE approach, C-spine immobilisation, CT head, neurosurgical referral if abnormal CT. Diffuse axonal injury: shearing of axons at grey-white matter junction, often no focal CT abnormality, poor prognosis.

title: Concussion – Features and management
content: Mild traumatic brain injury caused by biomechanical forces. Features: headache, dizziness, cognitive impairment ('brain fog'), memory problems, fatigue, sleep disturbance, emotional lability, photophobia, phonophobia. Symptoms typically resolve within 2–4 weeks. Post-concussion syndrome: symptoms persisting >3 months. Management: physical and cognitive rest initially, then graduated return to activity; avoid contact sports until symptom-free; no specific pharmacological treatment. Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE): progressive neurodegenerative disease from repeated head trauma.

title: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo – Features and management
content: Most common cause of vertigo. Caused by otoconia (calcium carbonate crystals) displaced into semicircular canals (usually posterior canal). Features: brief episodes of vertigo (<1 minute) triggered by head position changes (lying down, rolling over, looking up). Dix-Hallpike test: positive (upbeat-torsional nystagmus with latency, fatigable). Management: Epley manoeuvre (particle repositioning — highly effective, ~80% resolution with one treatment); Brandt-Daroff exercises (self-treatment). Spontaneous resolution common.

title: Anosmia – Causes and assessment
content: Loss of sense of smell. Causes: upper respiratory tract infection (most common — post-viral, including COVID-19), nasal polyps, head trauma (shearing of olfactory nerve fibres at cribriform plate), sinonasal disease, neurodegenerative disease (Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease — often early feature), congenital (Kallmann syndrome — anosmia + hypogonadotropic hypogonadism). Assessment: University of Pennsylvania Smell Identification Test (UPSIT), Sniffin' Sticks. Management: treat underlying cause; nasal steroid sprays for inflammatory causes; olfactory training (repeated exposure to strong odours).

title: Fasciculations – Causes and significance
content: Fasciculations are spontaneous contractions of a group of muscle fibres supplied by a single motor unit, visible through the skin. Causes: lower motor neuron disease (motor neurone disease — most important cause, also polio, Kennedy's disease), benign fasciculation syndrome (common, no weakness, normal EMG), electrolyte disturbances (hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia), thyrotoxicosis, drugs (lithium, corticosteroids). Significance: in the context of weakness and wasting → lower motor neuron pathology; isolated fasciculations without weakness → usually benign.

title: Ptosis – Causes and clinical approach
content: Drooping of the upper eyelid. Causes: CN III palsy (complete ptosis, eye deviated down and out, dilated pupil if posterior communicating artery aneurysm), Horner's syndrome (partial ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis), myasthenia gravis (fatigable, variable, bilateral), myotonic dystrophy (bilateral, associated myotonia), congenital (levator palpebrae weakness). Assessment: assess pupil size, eye movements, fatigability, other cranial nerve signs. Urgent investigation required if: associated dilated pupil (posterior communicating artery aneurysm — CT angiography/MRA).

title: Swallowing problems – Neurological causes
content: Dysphagia in neurological disease: motor neurone disease (bulbar palsy — LMN, or pseudobulbar palsy — UMN), myasthenia gravis (fatigable), Parkinson's disease (bradykinesia of swallowing muscles), stroke (pseudobulbar or bulbar palsy), multiple sclerosis, Guillain-Barré syndrome. Assessment: bedside swallowing assessment, videofluoroscopy (gold standard), FEES (fibreoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing). Management: modified diet/fluid consistency, nasogastric tube (short-term), PEG tube (long-term), speech and language therapy.

title: Speech and language problems – Types and causes
content: Dysphasia (aphasia): disorder of language. Broca's aphasia (expressive): non-fluent speech, good comprehension, poor repetition; lesion in left inferior frontal gyrus. Wernicke's aphasia (receptive): fluent but meaningless speech (jargon), poor comprehension, poor repetition; lesion in left posterior superior temporal gyrus. Global aphasia: all aspects affected; large left hemisphere lesion. Dysarthria: motor speech disorder — slurred speech, normal language content; causes: stroke, MS, MND, cerebellar disease. Dysphonia: voice disorder — hoarseness; causes: vocal cord palsy (recurrent laryngeal nerve), laryngeal pathology.

title: Urinary symptoms in neurological disease
content: Neurogenic bladder types: overactive/spastic bladder (UMN lesion above sacral cord — urgency, frequency, urge incontinence; causes: stroke, MS, Parkinson's disease, spinal cord injury above S2); underactive/flaccid bladder (LMN lesion at or below sacral cord — urinary retention, overflow incontinence; causes: cauda equina syndrome, peripheral neuropathy, diabetes); detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia (SCI between pontine micturition centre and sacral cord). Assessment: post-void residual volume (ultrasound), urodynamics. Management: overactive — anticholinergics (oxybutynin, tolterodine), beta-3 agonists (mirabegron), botulinum toxin; underactive — intermittent self-catheterisation.

title: Neck pain and stiffness – Neurological causes
content: Meningism (neck stiffness): meningitis, subarachnoid haemorrhage, encephalitis — Kernig's sign (inability to extend knee when hip flexed to 90°), Brudzinski's sign (involuntary hip flexion on passive neck flexion). Cervical spondylosis: degenerative disc and facet joint disease; neck pain, radiculopathy, myelopathy. Cervical disc prolapse: acute radiculopathy. Atlantoaxial instability: rheumatoid arthritis, Down's syndrome — risk of spinal cord compression. Torticollis: involuntary neck rotation/tilting; causes: muscle spasm, dystonia, congenital.

title: Back pain – Red flags and neurological causes
content: Red flags: age <20 or >55 years, trauma, constant progressive pain (not mechanical), thoracic pain, past history of malignancy, systemic steroids, drug abuse/HIV, unwell/weight loss, widespread neurological symptoms, structural deformity. Neurological causes: disc prolapse with radiculopathy, spinal stenosis (neurogenic claudication — bilateral leg pain/weakness on walking, relieved by sitting/flexion), cauda equina syndrome (emergency — saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention, bilateral leg weakness), spinal cord compression, spinal metastases.

title: Gait disorders – Neurological causes
content: Hemiplegic gait: circumduction of stiff extended leg; stroke, UMN lesion. Scissor gait: bilateral spastic legs crossing; cerebral palsy, bilateral UMN lesion. Steppage gait: foot drop, high stepping; peroneal nerve palsy, L4/L5 radiculopathy, CMT. Trendelenburg gait: hip dip to opposite side; hip abductor weakness. Parkinsonian gait: shuffling, small steps, reduced arm swing, festination. Cerebellar ataxic gait: broad-based, unsteady, veering. Sensory ataxic gait: broad-based, stamping, worse with eyes closed (Romberg's positive); posterior column disease.

title: Muscle pain and myalgia – Neurological causes
content: Inflammatory myopathies: polymyositis (proximal muscle weakness + pain, elevated CK, EMG myopathic, muscle biopsy — endomysial inflammation), dermatomyositis (as polymyositis + skin features: heliotrope rash, Gottron's papules, V-sign, shawl sign — associated with malignancy), inclusion body myositis (elderly males, distal > proximal weakness, poor response to immunosuppression). Rhabdomyolysis: muscle breakdown → myoglobinuria → AKI; causes: trauma, exercise, drugs (statins, alcohol), seizures, infection. Fibromyalgia: widespread musculoskeletal pain, fatigue, sleep disturbance, cognitive symptoms; no objective weakness or CK elevation.

title: Behaviour and personality change – Neurological causes
content: Frontal lobe lesions: disinhibition, poor impulse control, perseveration, utilisation behaviour, executive dysfunction, personality change. Temporal lobe lesions: memory impairment, emotional changes, Klüver-Bucy syndrome (bilateral — hyperorality, hypersexuality, docility). Limbic encephalitis: autoimmune (anti-NMDAR, anti-LGI1, anti-CASPR2), paraneoplastic; features: psychiatric symptoms, seizures, memory impairment, movement disorders. Prion disease (CJD): rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus, cerebellar ataxia, psychiatric symptoms. Huntington's disease: autosomal dominant, CAG repeat on chromosome 4; chorea, psychiatric symptoms, dementia.

title: Abnormal involuntary movements – Classification
content: Tremor: rhythmic oscillatory movement. Chorea: brief, irregular, non-repetitive, flowing movements (Huntington's, Sydenham's, drug-induced, hyperthyroidism). Athetosis: slow, writhing movements (cerebral palsy, Wilson's disease). Ballismus/hemiballismus: violent flinging movements of proximal limbs (subthalamic nucleus lesion). Dystonia: sustained muscle contractions causing abnormal postures (writer's cramp, torticollis, generalised). Myoclonus: sudden brief jerks (epilepsy, metabolic, post-anoxic). Tics: stereotyped, suppressible movements/vocalisations (Tourette's syndrome).

title: Developmental delay – Neurological assessment
content: Domains: gross motor, fine motor, speech/language, social/adaptive. Red flags: loss of previously acquired skills (regression — always investigate urgently), no babbling by 12 months, no single words by 16 months, no two-word phrases by 24 months, any loss of language or social skills at any age. Causes: genetic (Down's syndrome, fragile X, Rett syndrome), structural brain abnormality, metabolic (PKU, hypothyroidism), perinatal injury (HIE), infection (congenital CMV, toxoplasma), social deprivation. Investigations: chromosomal microarray, metabolic screen, MRI brain, hearing test.

title: Acute and chronic pain management – WHO analgesic ladder
content: WHO three-step analgesic ladder: Step 1 — non-opioid analgesics (paracetamol, NSAIDs) ± adjuvants; Step 2 — mild opioids (codeine, tramadol) ± non-opioids ± adjuvants; Step 3 — strong opioids (morphine, oxycodone, fentanyl) ± non-opioids ± adjuvants. Adjuvants: antidepressants (amitriptyline, duloxetine), anticonvulsants (gabapentin, pregabalin), corticosteroids, bisphosphonates (bone pain), ketamine (NMDA antagonist). Opioid side effects: constipation (prescribe laxatives routinely), nausea, sedation, respiratory depression, dependence.

title: Breathlessness in neurological disease
content: Neurological causes of respiratory failure: Guillain-Barré syndrome (ascending paralysis of respiratory muscles — monitor FVC), myasthenia gravis crisis, motor neurone disease (diaphragm weakness — use BiPAP), high cervical spinal cord injury (above C3–C5 — phrenic nerve), myopathies (muscular dystrophy, polymyositis). Assessment: FVC (most sensitive for neuromuscular respiratory failure — FVC <1 L or <20 mL/kg indicates need for ventilatory support), ABG (late changes), peak flow (less useful). Management: non-invasive ventilation (BiPAP), intubation if FVC <15 mL/kg or acute deterioration.

title: Confusion – Neurological causes and assessment
content: Acute confusion (delirium): acute onset, fluctuating, inattention, disorganised thinking, altered consciousness. Causes: PINCH ME — Pain, Infection, Nutrition, Constipation, Hydration, Medication, Environment/Endocrine. Neurological causes: encephalitis, meningitis, stroke, seizures (post-ictal), raised ICP, Wernicke's encephalopathy, subdural haematoma. Assessment: 4AT score (rapid delirium assessment), CAM (Confusion Assessment Method). Management: treat underlying cause, non-pharmacological measures (orientation, familiar faces, lighting), haloperidol/lorazepam only if severe agitation posing risk.

title: Decreased/loss of consciousness – Neurological assessment
content: Causes: vascular (stroke, SAH, subdural haematoma), metabolic (hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, uraemia, hepatic encephalopathy, hypercapnia), toxic (alcohol, drugs, CO poisoning), infective (meningitis, encephalitis, sepsis), traumatic (head injury), epileptic (post-ictal, non-convulsive status epilepticus). Assessment: AVPU scale, GCS, pupil responses, brainstem reflexes. Investigations: blood glucose (immediate), FBC, U&E, LFTs, TFTs, ABG, blood cultures, CT head, LP (if CT negative and meningitis/SAH suspected), EEG (if non-convulsive status suspected).

title: Dizziness – Differential diagnosis and approach
content: Vertigo (illusion of movement): peripheral (BPPV, vestibular neuritis, Ménière's disease, labyrinthitis) vs central (cerebellar stroke, MS, brainstem lesion). Presyncope (feeling of impending faint): cardiovascular causes, postural hypotension, vasovagal. Disequilibrium (unsteadiness without illusion of movement): cerebellar disease, proprioceptive loss, Parkinson's disease. Non-specific dizziness: anxiety, hyperventilation, medication side effects. Key differentiating features: onset (sudden vs gradual), duration (seconds/minutes/hours), triggers (positional vs spontaneous), associated symptoms (hearing loss, tinnitus, neurological symptoms).

title: Eye pain and discomfort – Neurological causes
content: Optic neuritis: pain behind eye (worse with movement), reduced vision, RAPD. Cluster headache: severe periorbital pain with autonomic features. Raised ICP: bilateral eye discomfort, papilloedema. Cavernous sinus thrombosis: periorbital oedema, proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, pain. Tolosa-Hunt syndrome: painful ophthalmoplegia due to granulomatous inflammation of cavernous sinus; responds to steroids. Migraine: periorbital pain. Herpes zoster ophthalmicus: vesicular rash in V1 distribution, eye involvement.

title: Acute change in or loss of vision – Neurological causes
content: Amaurosis fugax (transient monocular blindness): TIA of retinal artery (branch of ophthalmic artery from ICA); 'curtain descending' over vision; urgent assessment (ABCD2 score, carotid Doppler). Central retinal artery occlusion: sudden painless monocular blindness, cherry-red spot on fundoscopy. Homonymous hemianopia: posterior circulation stroke (occipital cortex or optic radiation). Bitemporal hemianopia: pituitary lesion compressing optic chiasm. Cortical blindness: bilateral occipital lobe infarction; pupils normal (afferent pathway intact). Anton's syndrome: cortical blindness with anosognosia (patient denies blindness).

title: Unsteadiness – Cerebellar causes and features
content: Cerebellar dysfunction features (DANISH): Dysdiadochokinesis, Ataxia (gait and limb), Nystagmus (horizontal, fast phase towards lesion), Intention tremor, Slurred speech (dysarthria/scanning speech), Hypotonia, past-pointing. Causes: acute — stroke (PICA/AICA), MS, alcohol intoxication, drugs (phenytoin, carbamazepine); subacute — MS relapse, paraneoplastic (anti-Yo, anti-Hu antibodies), Wernicke's; chronic — hereditary ataxias (Friedreich's, SCA), alcohol-related cerebellar degeneration, hypothyroidism. Investigations: MRI brain, paraneoplastic antibodies, genetic testing.

title: Altered sensation – Patterns and causes
content: Glove and stocking distribution: peripheral neuropathy (diabetes, alcohol, B12 deficiency). Dermatomal distribution: radiculopathy (disc prolapse, herpes zoster). Hemisensory loss: thalamic or cortical lesion (stroke). Sensory level: spinal cord lesion. Dissociated sensory loss: pain/temperature loss with preserved vibration/proprioception (syringomyelia, anterior cord syndrome) or vice versa (posterior column disease — subacute combined degeneration, tabes dorsalis). Saddle anaesthesia: cauda equina syndrome. Bilateral glove and stocking: polyneuropathy.

title: Limb weakness – Upper vs lower motor neuron
content: Upper motor neuron (UMN) signs: weakness, increased tone (spasticity), hyperreflexia, extensor plantar response (Babinski's sign), clonus, no wasting (or disuse atrophy only). Causes: stroke, MS, motor neurone disease, spinal cord compression, cerebral palsy. Lower motor neuron (LMN) signs: weakness, decreased/absent tone (flaccidity), hyporeflexia/areflexia, flexor plantar response, wasting, fasciculations. Causes: peripheral neuropathy, radiculopathy, motor neurone disease (LMN component), Guillain-Barré syndrome, polio.

title: Diplopia – Approach and causes
content: Monocular diplopia (persists with one eye closed): corneal/lens pathology, not neurological. Binocular diplopia (resolves with one eye closed): CN III palsy (vertical + horizontal, ptosis, dilated pupil), CN IV palsy (vertical, worse reading/stairs), CN VI palsy (horizontal, worse looking towards affected side), INO (horizontal, impaired adduction), myasthenia gravis (fatigable, variable), thyroid eye disease (restrictive myopathy — inferior rectus most commonly affected → upgaze limitation), orbital fracture (blowout — inferior rectus trapped → upgaze limitation).

title: Facial pain – Causes and management
content: Trigeminal neuralgia: paroxysmal electric shock-like pain in V2/V3 distribution, triggered by light touch; carbamazepine first-line. Atypical facial pain: constant, poorly localised, bilateral, not triggered; often associated with depression/anxiety; antidepressants may help. Dental causes: toothache, temporomandibular joint dysfunction. Sinusitis: dull ache over sinuses, worse on bending forward. Herpes zoster: burning pain in V1 distribution, vesicular rash. Postherpetic neuralgia: persistent pain after zoster rash resolves; amitriptyline, gabapentin, capsaicin cream. Cluster headache: severe periorbital pain with autonomic features.

title: Facial weakness – Upper vs lower motor neuron
content: Upper motor neuron (UMN) facial weakness: forehead spared (bilateral cortical representation of forehead), lower face contralateral weakness; causes: stroke, MS, tumour. Lower motor neuron (LMN) facial weakness: entire face affected including forehead; causes: Bell's palsy (most common), Ramsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster of geniculate ganglion — painful vesicles in ear, facial palsy, sensorineural hearing loss), parotid tumour, cholesteatoma, Lyme disease, sarcoidosis, Guillain-Barré syndrome.

title: Chronic fatigue syndrome – Pathophysiology and differential diagnosis
content: The exact pathophysiology of ME/CFS remains unclear. Proposed mechanisms include immune dysregulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, autonomic nervous system abnormality, and neuroinflammation. Post-exertional malaise (PEM) is the hallmark feature — a worsening of symptoms following physical, cognitive, or emotional exertion that was previously tolerable, typically delayed by 12–48 hours and lasting days or weeks. Differential diagnoses to exclude: anaemia, hypothyroidism, coeliac disease, diabetes mellitus, depression, sleep disorders (obstructive sleep apnoea), inflammatory conditions (SLE, rheumatoid arthritis), malignancy.

title: Chronic fatigue syndrome – Investigations
content: ME/CFS is a clinical diagnosis — there is no specific diagnostic test. Investigations are performed to exclude other conditions. Recommended bloods: FBC, ESR, CRP, U&E, LFTs, TFTs, fasting glucose, calcium, creatine kinase, ferritin, coeliac antibodies, urine dipstick. Additional tests if clinically indicated: ANA, immunoglobulins, serology (EBV, CMV, Lyme disease). Normal results support the diagnosis of ME/CFS but do not confirm it.

title: Extradural haemorrhage – Pathophysiology and CT findings
content: Extradural (epidural) haematoma most commonly results from rupture of the middle meningeal artery following temporal or temporoparietal skull fracture. Blood accumulates between the skull and the dura mater. Because the dura is firmly adherent at suture lines, the haematoma is limited and forms a characteristic biconvex (lenticular) shape on CT. The haematoma does not cross suture lines. CT head shows a hyperdense biconvex collection, typically in the temporal region, with midline shift and mass effect. Herniation (uncal) may occur rapidly.

title: Extradural haemorrhage – Prognosis and complications
content: Prognosis is generally excellent if surgical evacuation is performed promptly before significant neurological deterioration. Mortality is <5% with timely treatment. Poor prognostic factors: GCS <8 on presentation, pupillary abnormalities (indicating herniation), large haematoma volume, significant midline shift. Complications: cerebral herniation (uncal — CN III palsy, contralateral hemiplegia), raised ICP, seizures, cerebral oedema, re-accumulation of haematoma.

title: Malaria – Diagnosis and prevention
content: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium species (falciparum, vivax, ovale, malariae, knowlesi). P. falciparum is the most dangerous, causing cerebral malaria and severe disease. Diagnosis: thick and thin blood films (gold standard — repeated every 12–24 hours if initial negative), rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs — detect Plasmodium antigens), PCR (most sensitive). Prevention: ABCD — Awareness of risk, Bite avoidance (DEET, long sleeves, bed nets), Chemoprophylaxis (atovaquone-proguanil, doxycycline, mefloquine — choice depends on destination), Diagnosis and treatment promptly.

title: Malaria – Non-cerebral complications
content: Severe P. falciparum malaria complications: acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), acute kidney injury (haemoglobinuria — 'blackwater fever'), severe anaemia (haemolysis), thrombocytopaenia, hypoglycaemia (quinine stimulates insulin release), hyperparasitaemia (>5% red cells infected), circulatory collapse/shock ('algid malaria'), disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), splenic rupture (especially P. vivax). Hyperreactive malarial splenomegaly: chronic immune response, massive splenomegaly, high IgM.

title: Spinal fracture – ASIA impairment scale
content: The American Spinal Injury Association (ASIA) impairment scale grades spinal cord injury: A — complete (no motor or sensory function preserved in S4–S5); B — sensory incomplete (sensory but not motor preserved below level, including S4–S5); C — motor incomplete (motor preserved below level, >50% key muscles grade <3); D — motor incomplete (motor preserved below level, ≥50% key muscles grade ≥3); E — normal (motor and sensory function normal). Used to guide prognosis and rehabilitation planning.

title: Spinal fracture – Investigations
content: Plain X-ray: initial assessment; may miss significant injuries. CT spine: gold standard for bony injury; performed in all patients with suspected spinal fracture or high-energy mechanism. MRI spine: best for soft tissue, ligamentous injury, spinal cord, and nerve root assessment; essential if neurological deficit present. NEXUS criteria (can clear C-spine clinically without imaging): no midline tenderness, no focal neurological deficit, normal alertness, no intoxication, no distracting injury.

title: Subdural haemorrhage – Pathophysiology
content: Subdural haematoma results from tearing of bridging veins that run between the cortical surface and the dural venous sinuses. Blood accumulates between the dura and the arachnoid mater. Because the subdural space is not bounded by suture lines, blood can spread freely across the entire cerebral hemisphere. Acute subdural haematoma: typically associated with significant underlying brain injury; high mortality (~60%). Chronic subdural haematoma: common in elderly patients (cerebral atrophy increases bridging vein tension), alcoholics, and patients on anticoagulants; blood liquefies over weeks.

title: Tension headache – Features and management
content: Most common headache type. Features: bilateral, pressing/tightening (non-pulsating) quality, mild-moderate intensity, not aggravated by routine physical activity, no nausea/vomiting (though photophobia or phonophobia may be present — but not both). Duration: 30 minutes to 7 days. Episodic (<15 days/month) vs chronic (≥15 days/month). Management: acute — aspirin, paracetamol, or NSAIDs (not opioids); prophylaxis (if frequent/chronic) — amitriptyline (first-line), mirtazapine, venlafaxine; non-pharmacological: stress management, physiotherapy, acupuncture.

title: Brain metastases – Prognosis and palliative care
content: Prognosis of brain metastases depends on: primary tumour type, number and size of metastases, performance status, systemic disease control, age. Recursive Partitioning Analysis (RPA) and Graded Prognostic Assessment (GPA) are used for prognostication. Median survival: 4–6 months overall; better prognosis for single metastasis with controlled primary (surgical resection + radiotherapy). Palliative care: symptom control (dexamethasone for oedema/headache, anticonvulsants for seizures), psychological support, advance care planning, hospice referral when appropriate.

title: Metastatic spinal cord compression – Epidemiology and presentation
content: Occurs in ~5–10% of cancer patients. Most common primary tumours: breast, lung, prostate, kidney, myeloma, lymphoma. Most common site: thoracic spine (70%), followed by lumbar (20%) and cervical (10%). Back pain is the earliest and most common symptom (present in >95%), typically worse lying flat (unlike mechanical back pain), and may precede neurological symptoms by weeks to months. Neurological symptoms: limb weakness, sensory disturbance, bladder/bowel dysfunction. Urgent MRI whole spine is mandatory.

title: Parkinson's disease – Non-motor features
content: Non-motor features are common and often more disabling than motor symptoms. Neuropsychiatric: depression (most common, ~40%), anxiety, apathy, psychosis (hallucinations — often visual, illusions), dementia (Parkinson's disease dementia — occurs >1 year after motor onset, unlike Lewy body dementia). Autonomic: postural hypotension, constipation, urinary urgency/frequency, erectile dysfunction, excessive sweating. Sleep: REM sleep behaviour disorder (acting out dreams — may precede motor symptoms by years), excessive daytime sleepiness, insomnia. Sensory: pain, anosmia (often early), paraesthesia.

title: Epilepsy – Driving and social implications
content: DVLA regulations: Group 1 (car/motorcycle) — must not drive for 1 year after any seizure; may resume if seizure-free for 1 year. Group 2 (HGV/bus) — must be seizure-free for 10 years off medication, or 5 years on medication with specialist support. Provoked seizures (e.g. due to acute illness): 6 months off driving (Group 1). First unprovoked seizure: 6 months off driving if no EEG/imaging abnormality. Employment: patients should be advised about safety-critical occupations (working at heights, operating heavy machinery, swimming). Contraception: enzyme-inducing antiepileptics reduce efficacy of combined oral contraceptive pill.

title: Epilepsy – Investigations
content: EEG: supports diagnosis but does not confirm or exclude epilepsy; inter-ictal EEG may be normal; video telemetry (prolonged EEG with video) is gold standard for seizure characterisation. MRI brain: preferred over CT; identifies structural causes (hippocampal sclerosis, cortical dysplasia, tumours, vascular malformations). CT head: used acutely if MRI unavailable or contraindicated. Blood tests: glucose, electrolytes, calcium, magnesium (to exclude metabolic causes). Serum prolactin: elevated after generalised tonic-clonic seizure (within 20 minutes); not routinely recommended.

title: Stroke – Haemorrhagic stroke management
content: Intracerebral haemorrhage (ICH): reverse anticoagulation urgently (vitamin K + prothrombin complex concentrate for warfarin; idarucizumab for dabigatran; andexanet alfa for factor Xa inhibitors). Blood pressure lowering: target systolic <140 mmHg within 1 hour if presenting BP 150–220 mmHg (INTERACT2 trial). Surgical evacuation: considered for cerebellar haemorrhage >3 cm causing hydrocephalus or brainstem compression; superficial lobar haemorrhage in young patients. Avoid antiplatelet/anticoagulant therapy acutely. Restart anticoagulation for AF after 4 weeks if high thromboembolic risk.

title: Stroke – Rehabilitation and complications
content: Early mobilisation and multidisciplinary rehabilitation (physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech and language therapy, neuropsychology). Stroke unit care reduces mortality and dependency. Post-stroke complications: spasticity (baclofen, botulinum toxin), shoulder pain (physiotherapy, intra-articular steroid), depression (~30% — SSRIs), central post-stroke pain (amitriptyline, pregabalin), epilepsy (~10%), dysphagia (modified diet, PEG if prolonged), DVT/PE (LMWH after haemorrhagic stroke excluded, compression stockings), pressure sores, urinary incontinence.

title: Multiple sclerosis – Prognosis and prognostic factors
content: Poor prognostic factors: male sex, older age at onset, primary progressive course, high relapse rate in early disease, incomplete recovery from relapses, motor/cerebellar symptoms at onset (vs sensory/visual), high T2 lesion load on MRI, spinal cord lesions. Good prognostic factors: female sex, young age at onset, relapsing-remitting course, sensory or visual symptoms at onset, complete recovery from relapses. Approximately 50% of patients with RR-MS will need a walking aid within 15 years. Life expectancy is reduced by ~7 years compared to the general population.

title: Peripheral nerve injuries – Seddon and Sunderland classifications
content: Seddon classification: Neuropraxia — focal demyelination, axon intact, full recovery expected (days to weeks); Axonotmesis — axon disrupted but endoneurium intact, Wallerian degeneration, recovery possible (months, ~1 mm/day); Neurotmesis — complete nerve division, poor recovery without surgical repair. Sunderland classification (5 grades): Grade I (neuropraxia), Grade II (axonotmesis, endoneurium intact), Grade III (endoneurium disrupted, perineurium intact), Grade IV (perineurium disrupted, epineurium intact), Grade V (complete nerve division/neurotmesis).

title: Myasthenia gravis – Cholinergic crisis vs myasthenic crisis
content: Myasthenic crisis: severe exacerbation of myasthenia gravis with respiratory failure; precipitated by infection, surgery, medication changes, or omission of medication. Management: IVIG or plasma exchange, ventilatory support, treat precipitant. Cholinergic crisis: excessive acetylcholinesterase inhibitor medication → excess ACh at nicotinic and muscarinic receptors. Features: SLUDGE (Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defaecation, GI distress, Emesis) + muscle weakness/fasciculations. Management: stop pyridostigmine, atropine (for muscarinic effects), ventilatory support. Differentiation: Tensilon test (edrophonium) — improves myasthenic crisis, worsens cholinergic crisis.

title: Encephalitis – Autoimmune encephalitis
content: Autoimmune encephalitis is increasingly recognised as a cause of encephalopathy. Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis: most common autoimmune encephalitis; associated with ovarian teratoma (young women); features — psychiatric symptoms (anxiety, psychosis), seizures, movement disorders (orofacial dyskinesias), autonomic instability, decreased consciousness; CSF: lymphocytic pleocytosis; MRI: may be normal or show T2 changes in medial temporal lobes; treatment: immunotherapy (steroids, IVIG, plasma exchange) + tumour removal. Anti-LGI1 encephalitis: faciobrachial dystonic seizures (pathognomonic), hyponatraemia, memory impairment.

title: Dementias – Reversible causes
content: Potentially reversible causes of dementia should always be excluded: hypothyroidism (TSH), B12/folate deficiency, neurosyphilis (VDRL/TPHA), normal pressure hydrocephalus (triad: dementia, gait, incontinence), subdural haematoma, brain tumour, depression ('pseudodementia'), alcohol-related dementia (Korsakoff's syndrome), Wilson's disease (young patients), HIV-associated dementia. Investigations: FBC, U&E, LFTs, TFTs, B12/folate, calcium, glucose, syphilis serology, HIV test (if risk factors), CT/MRI brain.

title: Transient ischaemic attack – Investigations and management
content: Investigations: brain imaging (MRI DWI preferred — may show small infarct even in 'TIA'), carotid Doppler (if anterior circulation symptoms), ECG and 24-hour cardiac monitoring (AF), echocardiogram (if cardioembolic source suspected), bloods (FBC, lipids, glucose, clotting). Management: aspirin 300 mg immediately (unless haemorrhage excluded), then clopidogrel 75 mg long-term. Carotid endarterectomy: within 2 weeks if 50–99% symptomatic stenosis (NASCET criteria). Blood pressure control, statin therapy, lifestyle modification. Dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + clopidogrel) for 21 days after high-risk TIA (POINT/CHANCE trials).

title: Acoustic neuroma – Investigations and bilateral disease
content: Investigations: MRI internal auditory meatus with gadolinium (investigation of choice — shows enhancing mass in internal auditory canal/cerebellopontine angle); pure tone audiogram (sensorineural hearing loss); auditory brainstem response (ABR — delayed or absent wave V). Bilateral acoustic neuromas are pathognomonic of neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2) — autosomal dominant, mutation in NF2 gene on chromosome 22 (merlin protein). NF2 patients also develop other CNS tumours (meningiomas, ependymomas, schwannomas of other cranial and spinal nerves).

title: Febrile convulsion – Management and prognosis
content: Acute management: place in recovery position, protect from injury, do not restrain. If seizure lasts >5 minutes: buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam. Investigate for source of fever (FBC, CRP, blood cultures, urine MC&S). LP: consider if <18 months (meningism signs may be absent), or if meningitis/encephalitis cannot be excluded. Prognosis: recurrence risk ~30% (higher if: age <18 months, family history, brief duration of fever before seizure, low-grade fever). Risk of developing epilepsy: ~2–4% (compared to 1% in general population). Risk factors for epilepsy: complex febrile convulsion (prolonged >15 min, focal, or multiple within 24 hours), neurological abnormality, family history of epilepsy.

title: Diabetic neuropathy – Management
content: Prevention: optimal glycaemic control (reduces risk and slows progression), blood pressure control, smoking cessation. Symptomatic management of painful diabetic neuropathy (NICE): first-line — duloxetine (preferred if depression co-exists), amitriptyline, pregabalin, or gabapentin (as monotherapy; switch if ineffective rather than combining). Second-line: combination of first-line agents. Tramadol: for acute rescue only. Topical capsaicin cream: localised neuropathic pain. Foot care: regular podiatry, protective footwear, patient education on foot inspection. Autonomic neuropathy: postural hypotension (fludrocortisone, midodrine), gastroparesis (metoclopramide, erythromycin), erectile dysfunction (PDE5 inhibitors).

title: Raised intracranial pressure – Herniation syndromes
content: Uncal (transtentorial) herniation: medial temporal lobe herniates through tentorium cerebelli; compresses CN III (ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil), then contralateral corticospinal tract (contralateral hemiplegia), then bilateral motor signs; Kernohan's notch phenomenon — contralateral cerebral peduncle compressed against tentorium → ipsilateral hemiplegia (false localising sign). Tonsillar herniation: cerebellar tonsils herniate through foramen magnum; compresses medulla → Cushing's triad (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular respirations), respiratory arrest. Subfalcine herniation: cingulate gyrus herniates under falx cerebri; may compress ACA → leg weakness.
